- **A shared secret rather than a signature on the webhook**, and the difference is stated rather than glossed: Twilio signs its payloads, most inbound-email providers offer only a secret. The mitigation is what the endpoint can do — file a message into an existing conversation or into the unrouted queue, and nothing else. 403 on a bad secret so it is not retried; 503 when unconfigured so it is; 500 on a failure because losing the message means a tenant told us something we never recorded.
- **An unset inbound domain is a supported state.** Without one, no reply keys are minted and replies route by From: address — R-017's ordinary path. What is lost is thread precision, not the feature.

**Found along the way.** Nothing broken, but two near-misses worth the tests that caught them: a key containing a `+` would have been silently truncated by the obvious `split('+')[1]`, and a lookalike domain would have routed if the host check had been loose. Both have their own test.

**What it left behind.**
- **No provider is wired.** The webhook parses a normalized payload in one place (D-7's rule), but which provider posts to it is a deployment decision, and `INBOUND_EMAIL_SECRET`/`INBOUND_EMAIL_ADDRESS` are unset by default so the endpoint refuses everything until somebody configures it.
- **Attachments are dropped.** A tenant photographing a leak and emailing it gets their words filed and their picture discarded silently. R-019 already has the upload path for a maintenance photo; wiring the two together is a real item and nothing owns it.
- **No inbound-email opt-out.** SMS has `STOP` handling (R-040e) and email has no equivalent here — a tenant replying "stop emailing me" threads like any other message and changes nothing about what we send.
- **HTML-only email is stored empty.** The route prefers the plain-text part and does not strip HTML, so a client that sent only HTML files a blank message. Better than storing markup, worse than converting it, and the fix is a converter nobody needs yet.

## R-097d — An inbound email keeps what it carried
**Commit:** `2fe6393`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it built.** `htmlToText` in core with 6 tests; `inbound-attachments.ts` — the trust-boundary rules for accepting a file from a stranger; `Document.messageId` and `UnroutedMessage.attachmentsDropped`; attachments rendered on the thread and the dropped count on the triage queue; 4 more database tests.

**Why it existed.** R-097a named both of these as gaps in its own PROGRESS entry the same day. They are better described as defects: a tenant photographing a leak and emailing it got their sentence recorded and their evidence discarded, silently; and a client that sent only HTML filed a blank message, so somebody who typed a paragraph got a record saying they said nothing.

**What it decided.** Recorded as **D-126**.

- **The HTML converter is not a parser and adds no dependency.** It only ever deletes — script and style contents whole, then every tag — and the result goes into an append-only body that React renders as text, so the worst a hostile input can produce is nonsense somebody reads. Unrecognised entities are left as written: a visible `&hellip;` is a cosmetic blemish, a wrong guess is a changed sentence in an evidence trail. Plain text still wins where it exists, because that is what the sender's own client thought the words were.
- **An attachment arrives from an unauthenticated stranger**, and every rule follows from that. A closed type list — images and PDFs, what tenants and vendors actually send — rather than a block list somebody has to keep ahead of. A size cap *and* a count cap, because without both one message is an unbounded write to somebody else's storage bill. The declared content type is recorded because it is what the sender claimed, and trusted for nothing else: nothing here executes, renders or parses the bytes. And the filename is sanitised for **display** as well as for the storage key, which `generateStorageKey` already handled — `invoice.pdf.exe` from a stranger should not read as an invoice on a staff screen.
- **An image is `MAINTENANCE_PHOTO`, a PDF is `OTHER`.** The first matches R-019's own type for the same thing arriving through the portal — a photograph of a leak is the same evidence whichever way it was sent. The second is deliberately unguessed: a PDF is as often an invoice as anything else, and guessing would attach a wrong retention rule (DOC-05).
- **Nothing is stored for an unrouted message, and the drop is visible.** A `Document` must have a property; an unrouted message has none, and inventing one is exactly the guess `decideRoute` refuses. So the count goes on the row and the triage queue says a photograph was sent and could not be kept, with the instruction to ask for it again. Fixing only the routed half would have left the original defect — silent loss — in the harder one.
- **Attachment storage can never fail the message.** By the time it runs the words are already recorded, which is the half that matters; a storage outage must not lose what somebody said as well as what they attached.
- **`Document.messageId`, not a join table.** CLAUDE.md's rule is that late association with an append-only row needs a join table (`WorkOrderMessageLink` exists for exactly that). This association is not late: the document is written knowing its message, so the FK goes on the mutable side and `Message` is never amended.

**Found along the way.** Nothing broken. Worth noting that a `prisma format` failure is silent under `tail -1` — the same trap as R-094b, hit again while adding these columns: the migration applied and the schema was left incomplete, caught only because `db:drift` disagreed. The drift check is doing real work in this repo.

**What it left behind.**
- **No inbound-email opt-out.** SMS honours `STOP` (R-040e); email has no equivalent, so a tenant replying "stop emailing me" threads like any other message and changes nothing about what we send. The clearest remaining gap in inbound email, and nothing owns it.
- **Attachments are not linked to a ticket.** An emailed photo lands on the message and on the property; R-019's portal path attaches one to a *ticket*, which is what makes it show on the job. Whoever wires SMS-to-ticket's sibling for email should do both at once.
- **No virus scanning.** Files from strangers are stored and served back to staff. The type and size caps narrow it; a scanner is a vendor decision nobody has made.

## R-097e — Email honours "stop emailing me"
**Commit:** `d7e5bbc`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it built.** `isEmailOptOutRequest` and `emailOptOutConfirmation` in core with 8 tests; `email-opt-out.ts`, which switches off every email preference a recipient is allowed to switch off and confirms what is left; the webhook wiring; `CATEGORY_LABELS` moved from a client component into core; 2 more database tests.

**Why it existed.** SMS has honoured `STOP` since R-040e. Email honoured nothing, so a tenant replying "please stop emailing me" got a message threaded and no change to what we sent them — named as the clearest unowned gap when R-097d shipped.

**What it decided.** Recorded as **D-127**.

- **An email opt-out is not an SMS `STOP`, and treating it as one is wrong in both directions.** `STOP` is a single token with legal force the *carrier* enforces — it blocks the number, which is why `optOutReply` deliberately sends no confirmation. Email has no carrier and no command grammar: people write a sentence, and nobody else enforces anything.
- **So the false-positive trade-off inverts.** `classifyOptOutKeyword` is deliberately generous, because filing "STOP the leak" as a repair risks continuing to text somebody who asked us not to. Here the expensive mistake is the opposite: a tenant whose rent reminders were silently switched off because they wrote "stop" in a sentence about a dripping tap gets a late fee. Every phrase is multi-word and unambiguous, `stop` alone is deliberately not one of them, and there is a test full of real maintenance sentences that must not match.
- **Detection reads the stripped body.** Almost every marketing email ever sent carries "unsubscribe" in its footer, so a reply quoting one would otherwise opt somebody out every single time. There is a test for exactly that, asserting the raw body *would* have matched and the stripped one does not.
- **The dangerous outcome is not "we kept emailing them".** Four categories are locked on by NOTIF-02 and no request can switch them off — a legal notice that did not arrive is a notice that was not served, and an entry notice is an obligation of ours rather than a subscription of theirs. The failure to avoid is a tenant who believes they switched off every email, misses an entry notice, and finds somebody in their home, **having been misled by us**.
- **Hence one more email after being asked for none.** That is the standard shape and it earns the intrusion by naming exactly what will still arrive, in `LOCKED_CATEGORIES`' own words — NOTIF-02 already requires that reason be shown wherever the question is asked, and this is one of the places it is asked.
- **Sent through `deliverOverChannel`, not `notify()`.** Routing it through the preference engine would let the message announcing a preference change be suppressed by the change it announces. The kill switch and sandbox redirect still apply, because they live in `deliverOverChannel` and cover everything.
- **Email only.** An opt-out arriving by email says nothing about whether somebody wants a text at midnight about a burst pipe; reading it as portfolio-wide silence is a far larger inference than the sentence supports.
- **The message stays in the conversation** rather than being swallowed by the command — R-040e's rule for a `STOP` text, and for the same reason: an evidence trail that quietly drops the one message that changed what we may send is not an evidence trail.
- **`CATEGORY_LABELS` moved into core.** The confirmation needs the same words as the settings screen, and two copies of a vocabulary is one copy that eventually stops matching — the call `LOCKED_CATEGORIES` already made about its explanations. The exhaustive `Record` still makes a new category a compile error.

**What it left behind.**
- **No way back except replying.** The confirmation says to reply and somebody will turn them on again; there is no one-click resubscribe link, which would need another token purpose. A staff member has to act on the reply.
- **Nothing tells staff it happened.** The preferences change and the confirmation goes out, but no task is raised and the thread shows only the tenant's own message. Whoever wants "who has muted us" needs a report, and none exists.
- **A guarantor cannot opt out this way.** Routing resolves a tenant or a vendor, and a guarantor emailing in is unrouted — so their request lands in triage like any other unmatched message.

## R-097f — Email opens maintenance tickets
**Commit:** `f0d8093`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it built.** `decideEmailIntake` and `formatEmailTicketDescription` in core with 6 tests; `email-intake.ts`, the sibling of `sms-intake.ts`; the webhook rewired through it; emailed attachments now hung off the ticket as well as the message; 5 more database tests.

**Why it existed.** R-021 has turned an inbound text from a tenant into a maintenance ticket since the MVP. Email did none of it — somebody emailing "my boiler is broken" got a threaded conversation and nothing in anybody's work queue. `TicketSource.EMAIL` has existed in the schema the whole time with nothing writing it.

**What it decided.** Recorded as **D-128**.

- **R-021's shape verbatim, including the ordering.** Thread first through `receiveInboundMessage`, then consider a ticket — because a message that cannot be routed must never open one. A ticket has to belong to a property and a tenant, and inventing either is exactly what `decideRoute` refuses to do. A test asserts an unroutable email opens nothing.
- **The one real difference is that email is a conversation.** Nobody texts their property manager to say "thanks", so R-021's rule — any text from a tenant with nothing open becomes a ticket — is right for SMS. Applied verbatim to email, every "Thursday works" becomes a maintenance ticket and the triage queue R-023 depends on stops being real.
- **The distinction is drawn on evidence, never on what the words look like.** A reply key is proof they hit reply on something of ours; recent outbound in the same conversation is good enough when a corporate mail system stripped the tag. Guessing "is this a complaint?" from prose would be the same mistake `formatSmsTicketDescription` already refuses one level down, where it declines to guess a *category* because a wrong label on the one intake path with no clarifying prompts is worse than no label. Fourteen days for the reply window, stated where it is defined: long enough that a slow answer is still an answer, short enough that an email three months later is somebody telling us something new.
- **An opt-out is not a repair.** R-097e's check runs before the ticket decision, because a maintenance ticket titled "please unsubscribe me" is the visible half of getting that wrong.
- **The photograph is hung off the ticket, not only the message.** R-097d stored it against the message, which is where it belongs; without this the person dispatched to fix the leak never sees the picture.
- **The description tells triage something different from the SMS one.** An emailer *can* be asked a follow-up question, at length, and may well have attached something — so the closing line says to reply by email and check the conversation, where the text version says to reply by text and warns the sender may never open the portal.

**What it left behind.**
- **No category, deliberately**, matching SMS. R-023's triage assigns it from a human reading the words, and R-019's structured intake is the only path that earns one by asking.
- **The reply window is a constant, not configuration.** Fourteen days is a guess with reasoning attached rather than a measurement; if a portfolio finds it wrong, it is one number in core with a test beside it.
- **A vendor emailing about a job opens nothing**, matching SMS — their messages thread and stop there. R-025's magic link is the vendor's real surface, and a vendor saying "running late" is not a maintenance request from a tenant.
- **Nothing links an emailed ticket back to the message thread on screen.** The ticket carries the tenant's words in its description and the photo is attached, but a reader on the ticket cannot jump to the conversation. R-032's `WorkOrderMessageLink` is the shape that would fix it.

## Demo checkpoint 3 — Golden Path 3, defined and walked
**Commit:** `f3baa47`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it did.** Defined the demo checkpoint Milestone 8 never had, wrote it as a kept spec (`e2e/golden-path-3.spec.ts`) rather than a manual pass, walked it, and fixed what it found. Recorded as **D-129** and **D-130**.

**The first finding was the absence itself.** D-28 says every checkpoint line is an acceptance gate for the milestone above it and gets walked before the next milestone's items start. Milestone 8 — twelve risk items, R-083 through R-091c — closed with no checkpoint at all. That is the exact condition D-28 exists to prevent, and the same one that let checkpoint 1's four seam defects through.

**The path crosses six items that each promise something does not leak** — R-091, R-091b, R-091c, R-094b, R-092, R-097c — and asserts each promise from *outside* the item that made it: an owner opens a confidential case, orders the re-key, removes the restricted party without their signature, records the statutory early termination, and then the audit trail, the locksmith's work order, a manager's own screens, the handoff packet and the calendar feed are each checked for what they show. All five product promises held.

**What did not hold was the sweep, and one of the walk's own assertions.**

- **Nine e2e specs shared one login rate-limit bucket (D-130).** R-003 limits staff sign-in to ten attempts per IP per five minutes; local e2e traffic carries no `x-forwarded-for`, so every spec without one shared a single bucket. Past roughly the two-hundredth test of a full sweep, the eleventh login in five minutes starts being refused — and **the symptom looks nothing like the cause**: `page.waitForURL` times out sixty seconds after clicking "Sign in", inside whichever spec happened to be running. Both failures in the first full sweep were in notice specs; neither had anything to do with notices, and both passed in isolation, which is exactly the shape that gets written off as flakiness. Several specs had already solved it inline, which is why it stayed invisible — the pattern existed, it just was not everywhere. Now `uniqueClientHeaders()` in `e2e/fixtures.ts`, applied to the nine that lacked it **and to every `browser.newContext()` call site**, which is the half even the specs that had remembered got wrong: a new context does not inherit `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders`. **Two of the nine were written in this same session**, which is the argument for a helper over a convention.
- **The walk's own first assertion was wrong, twice over.** It initially demanded a manager get a 404 on the confidential case — but a manager holds no `confidential.read` at all, so the guard *redirects* to `/no-access`, which returns a healthy 200. That is R-103's recorded lesson, caught by reading rather than by running. Then it demanded the restricted party's name not appear on the lease page, which failed immediately and correctly: Sam is an occupant of the unit and an outgoing party on a lease amendment, both facts a manager running the property can obviously see. R-091b's design is that the *change* is visible and its *reason* is not, and conflating the person with the case would have made the spec demand something the product must not do — hide a lease party from the person managing the lease. The spec now asserts the case content, the absence of the "open a case" control, and the presence of D-112's neutral amendment reason.
- **A dynamic `await import()` breaks under Playwright's ESM handling.** Every other spec imports from `@rental/core/auth` statically; this one now does too.

**And the confirming sweep found a third test defect — a latent race, months old.** `993 passed, 8 skipped, 1 flaky`, reconciling exactly against the 1000 listed plus Golden Path 3's two. The one flaky was `vendor-invoice-splits.spec.ts` reading a tax-export CSV that still contained a work order a vendor-invoice split should have claimed. It does not reproduce in isolation across four repeats, and the cause is **`waitForURL` on the page it was already on**: the form lives at `/money/vendor-invoices`, so `waitForURL('**/money/vendor-invoices')` after clicking Record resolved instantly and the CSV fetch raced the write. That is CLAUDE.md's "an assertion that is already true" in a costume harder to recognise, because a `waitForURL` *looks* like waiting. Now polls the split row — the fact the export actually reads — and passes 42/42 across three repeats. **Deliberately not written off as parallel-load flakiness**, which CLAUDE.md names as the diagnosis that has been missed three times; the sibling call site fifty lines above is safe precisely because it waits on rendered output rather than on a URL.

**What it left behind.**
- **Milestone 9 has no checkpoint either.** Phase 3 is being built item by item, and the same gap will open again. Whoever closes it should define one before the items, not after.
- **The walk is one path.** It covers the confidential chain because that is where six items' promises intersect; the money path (R-083's evictions, R-084's holds, R-087's abandonment) has no equivalent walk, and its items make promises of the same kind about what automation must not do to a protected tenancy.

## Demo checkpoint 4 — Golden Path 4, defined and walked
**Commits:** `0ad2013` (the walk) · `9f90339` (the defect it found)  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it did.** Defined the demo checkpoint Milestone 9 never had, wrote it as a kept spec (`e2e/golden-path-4.spec.ts`), walked it, and fixed the product defect it found on its first pass. Recorded as **D-131** and **D-132**.

**Defined before the milestone was declared closed, which is the half checkpoint 3 had to learn the hard way.** R-097f's own entry above already said Milestone 9 had no checkpoint and that whoever closed it should define one before the items rather than after. This is that, one milestone late instead of two.

**The thesis, and why it is a different question from checkpoint 3's.** Milestone 9 built two surfaces the outside world drives and neither of which can authenticate anybody: a smart-lockbox self-showing (R-094, R-094b) and inbound email (R-097a, R-097d, R-097e, R-097f). A stranger types a name into a page; a stranger sends a `From:` header. Both are as trustworthy as caller ID, and both are allowed to cause real things — a door opening, a maintenance ticket, a permanent line in somebody's evidence trail. So the walk asks **what an unauthenticated stranger is allowed to cause**, where checkpoint 3 asked what leaks.

One person is followed the whole way, and each item's promise is asserted against a surface that item does not own. She books a viewing on a vacant house → is refused when the name on the ID is not the name that booked it, leaving no access row at all → is let in when it is, with the code on a page and in no message (asserted at the notification engine) and no photo ID anywhere (asserted at the `Document` table) → the owner pulls the code and her next refresh loses it → **she moves in** → a fresh self-showing on the now-occupied unit is refused outright, without even offering the ID form, which is D-115's rule asserted against a state change *leasing* made → she is given her own door code, one per person, and the audit records that the door was programmed and never the code → she emails about a leaking boiler with a photograph, which threads, opens a ticket, and hangs the photograph off the **ticket** → she emails again asking to be unsubscribed, which switches off every email she is allowed to switch off, writes no preference row for the four NOTIF-02 locks, and opens no second ticket.

**The gate is the visit her own email caused.** The work order is scheduled and the entry notice goes to the address she just asked us to stop using, un-suppressed — because a locked category outranks any opt-out, and the outcome R-097e's own header names is a tenant who believes she switched everything off and finds somebody in her home. Then the job is marked complete and the "did we fix it?" follow-up is `SUPPRESSED / preference_off`. **Both halves, or neither proves anything:** if everything survived an opt-out then the opt-out does not work, and the contrast is what tells them apart. R-027 and R-097e were built four milestones apart and meet nowhere else in the suite.

**Unlike checkpoint 3, what it found was in the product, and it was serious (D-132).** The walk failed on its first pass at the email leg: `From: Dorothy Vaughan <d@example.com>` came back `unrouted`.

- **The `<…>` unwrap existed, on the wrong half.** `extractReplyKey` unwrapped the display-name form for the **recipient** list, where the reply key is. Nothing unwrapped it for **`From:`**, where the routing is — so `candidatesForEmail` compared the whole header value against `Tenant.email` and matched nothing.
- **Every real mail client sets a display name**, so in production this is not an edge case: it is the ordinary path, and the only path at all where no inbound domain is configured.
- **Four items were silently doing nothing.** R-097f opened no ticket, R-097d counted the photograph instead of keeping it, R-097e did not honour the opt-out — all of them downstream of a routing decision that had already given up.
- **And it is invisible**, which is why four items shipped over it. An unrouted message is what that queue is *for*: the failure looks exactly like mail from a stranger we cannot place. Every one of those items' own tests passed a bare address, because each was written from inside its own seam. This is the defect shape D-28 exists for, found the first time anything sent a `From:` header shaped the way a mail client shapes one.
- **Fixed as one expression, in core.** `emailAddressOnly()` in `packages/core/comms/email-reply.ts`, used by `extractReplyKey` *and* by the webhook's `From`, so the two halves can never disagree again. The webhook also stopped splitting `From:` on commas — that header is a single mailbox, and splitting it turned `"Vaughan, Dorothy" <d@example.com>` into `"Vaughan` a second way. Three unit tests beside it.
- **The general lesson**: a helper written for one caller, inside the item that needed it, is a helper the next caller does not know exists.

**What it built along the way.** `INBOUND_EMAIL_SECRET` is now set for the e2e web server in `playwright.config.ts`, exactly as `TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN` and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` already are and for the same reason — without it the route answers 503 to everything, correctly, and the whole email half of the walk would pass having proved nothing. `INBOUND_EMAIL_ADDRESS` is deliberately **not** set: it would put a `Reply-To` on every outbound email the suite sends, and the walk wants the From:-matching path anyway. Both variables are now documented by name in `.env.example`, which R-097a never added.

**What it left behind.**
- **The comma-split on `to`/`cc` is still there.** `"Last, First" <a@b>` in a recipient list still splits wrongly, so a reply key addressed alongside such a recipient can be missed. The consequence is a fall-through to From: matching — the documented graceful degradation — rather than a loss, so it is a real but bounded gap. A proper RFC 5322 address-list parser is the fix and is more than this walk should carry.
- **No walk of the money path.** Checkpoint 3 left this same note: R-083's evictions, R-084's holds and R-087's abandonment make promises of the same kind about what automation must not do to a protected tenancy, and nothing crosses them end to end.
- **Milestone 9 is the last milestone, and everything still unbuilt in it is gated** — R-093 on vendor partnerships, R-095 on one narrow owner question (D-123), R-097b on a vendor and the furnisher review D-4 already requires. So there is no next checkpoint to define yet; when a gate opens, define one before the item rather than after, which is the thing both 3 and 4 were written to stop repeating.

## Demo checkpoint 5 — Golden Path 5, the money path
**Commit:** `fb5b16c`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it did.** Wrote and walked the checkpoint that checkpoint 3 and checkpoint 4 both wrote down and neither did — `e2e/golden-path-5.spec.ts` — and fixed the product defect it found, plus a second defect the fix itself exposed. Recorded as **D-134**.

**The third time of asking.** Both earlier checkpoints end their "what it left behind" with the same sentence: the money path has no equivalent walk, and R-083's evictions, R-084's holds and R-087's abandonment make promises of the same kind about what automation must not do to a protected tenancy. Written now rather than deferred a third time.

**The thesis, and why it is neither of theirs.** Checkpoint 3 asked what leaks; checkpoint 4 asked what an unauthenticated stranger is allowed to cause. This one asks **when the law puts a fence around a tenancy, what must the collections machine stop doing — and what must the fence never forgive?** R-044 built the arrears chase in Milestone 4. R-084 built the fence in Milestone 8, four milestones later. R-085 built the one statute that raises it by itself. Each has a test proving its own half — `lib/holds/holds.test.ts` proves `leasesHalted` returns the right set, `scra.spec.ts` proves a certificate places the hold, `rent-roll.spec.ts` proves the chase chases — and **nothing joins the three**, which is precisely where an operator lives: one tenancy, over time, as its legal status changes underneath a screen somebody already has open.

So one tenancy is followed. She falls behind and is chased, lawfully and correctly (asserted at the notification engine, not at R-044's own screen). The rent roll is re-rendered, she is ticked, the template is chosen, and **nothing is pressed**. In a second browser context a DMDC certificate comes back `in_service` and the SCRA hold places itself — the only automatic hold in the product. **Then** the aimed press lands.

**The gate has two halves and needs both.** The press must refuse, which is the race R-084's own text claims to defend by name — "a hold placed while the screen was open stops the chase the same way a payment does" — and it must **say why**, because under 11 U.S.C. §362 or the SCRA the reason a chase was withheld is the record. Then the screen is reloaded: the chase is no longer on offer and the row says so, **and the balance is still $1,500.00 in its late bucket**. Either half alone passes for the wrong reason. If the debt vanished with the chase, the product would have forgiven something nobody decided to forgive; if the chase survived, it would have violated the stay while displaying a banner saying the stay was in force. Only the contrast tells a guard from an off switch.

**What it found was in the product, and it is two defects with one root (D-134).**

- **The guard refused and blamed the wrong thing.** `pastGraceLeaseIds` subtracts held leases from the same `Set` as paid ones and returns a bare set, so `sendReminders` could not tell them apart and reported both as *"not past the grace period"* — to the operator on screen, and permanently into the `message.bulk_sent` audit row. For a tenancy under an automatic stay that sentence is not unhelpful, it is **false**: it sends somebody looking for a payment that was never made, and it writes that fiction into the one record that is supposed to answer "why did this tenant not get the reminder we sent everybody". Fixed at the shared function's caller rather than at the message — `reminders.ts` now asks `leasesHalted` for the reason, so every skip is named for what it actually was.
- **And the screen went on offering the control.** `rentRoll()` was **never hold-aware at all** — only the send-time re-check was. So a held tenancy kept its checkbox, was counted in "select all N past grace", and gave no reason in its row. `rent-roll-table.tsx`'s own header states the rule it was quietly breaking: a row that is not chaseable gets **no control and a written reason**, because a control that looks available and refuses is worse than no control. `RentRollRow` now carries `chaseHeld`, deliberately **separate from `pastGrace`** so the debt stays visible, aged and owed while the asking stops.
- **Invisible from inside R-084**, which is the shape D-28 exists for. R-084's promise was that every guard asks `leasesHalted` for an effect and never names a hold type, and it kept that promise exactly. Nothing in it asked what the operator was *told*, because from inside the item the answer looked like "the chase was correctly refused" — which it was.

**The fix exposed a worse failure, and only running it found that.** With the last chaseable row held, `chaseable.length` goes to zero and the whole "Chase everyone past grace" panel unmounts — taking the `FieldError` and `LiveRegion` that carry the action's result with it. The refusal then rendered **nowhere**: press Send on a stale selection and the panel simply disappears, saying nothing at all, which is worse than the wrong reason this walk set out to fix. It is the self-replacing-panel trap R-086 documents, reached from a new direction. The result region is now always mounted while the user can send, outside the conditional panel, so `aria-live` has somewhere to announce into rather than arriving with the text already in it. **Had the walk stopped at "the message is now right", this would have shipped.**

**And the confirming unit run found a third defect — a latent global-count race, months old.** `inbound-email.test.ts`'s "never opens a ticket for a message nobody could route" took `prisma.ticket.count()` over the **whole shared database** before and after the call, so any other test file opening a ticket between the two counts turned it red. It passed in isolation every time it was asked and lost for the first time here (`expected 2812 to be 2811`). Same family as the two `state: 'ZZ'` files CLAUDE.md already records: a test that reads globally in a database other files are writing to. Now scoped to the two properties the file itself created — where a wrongly-opened ticket could actually land. **Deliberately not written off as parallel-load flakiness**, which CLAUDE.md names as the diagnosis missed three times; it was reproduced as a full-run-only failure and confirmed green in isolation before being changed.

**What it decided.**
- **`chaseHeld` is a separate field from `pastGrace`, not a mutation of it.** Collapsing them would have been the smaller diff and would have quietly dropped the tenancy out of the aging totals and the CSV — forgiving the debt on the report, which is the exact thing the walk's second half exists to catch.
- **The written reason for a held row deliberately does not contain the words "past grace".** `getByText` is a case-insensitive substring match, so a held row answering to that phrase would let a future test believe the chase was on offer. Noted next to the string.
- **The walk asserts the refusal at three surfaces** — the screen, the notification engine, and the audit row — because the first is transient, the second is what the tenant actually experiences, and only the third is still there in three weeks when somebody asks.

**What it left behind.**
- **The walk covers the collections half of the money path, not all of it.** R-083's eviction gates, R-087's abandonment refusals and R-086's accommodation clock each have their own gate spec, and re-running them inside a walk would be padding. What has no walk is the *crossing* of those with holds — an abandonment assessment on a tenancy under an SCRA hold, say — and no item currently claims that crossing.
- **`pastGraceLeaseIds` still returns a bare `Set`.** The caller now asks a second question to recover the reason, which is one extra query on a path that already does several. Making it return both sets is the tidier shape and ripples into `holds.test.ts`; not worth doing inside a checkpoint whose job was to find the defect.
- **No further checkpoint to define.** Milestone 9 is the last milestone and everything unbuilt in it is gated on a vendor or on the furnisher review D-4 already requires. When a gate opens, define the checkpoint before the item — the thing 3, 4 and 5 were each written to stop repeating.

## Inbound email: a recipient list is split quote-aware
**Commit:** `d24f2e0`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it built.** `splitAddressList` in `packages/core/comms/email-reply.ts`, and the webhook's `addresses()` now uses it instead of `value.split(',')`. Recorded as **D-135**.

**Closing the gap D-132 named rather than a new discovery.** Golden Path 4 fixed `From:` — one mailbox, never split — and its PROGRESS entry ended by saying `To:`/`Cc:` still split naively, that a reply key addressed alongside `"Last, First" <a@b>` could therefore be missed, and that a proper parser was more than that walk should carry. This is that, and it is the last unbuilt thing in the repo that is not gated on a vendor.

**What the naive split actually costs, which is not the mangled name.** `"Vaughan, Dorothy" <d@example.com>, hello+<key>@inbound.example.com` split on every comma yields `"Vaughan` and `Dorothy" <d@example.com>` and the key — two fragments that each look like a real recipient, and nothing downstream can tell they are debris. **The loss is the reply key**, which is the only high-confidence match inbound email has: it names the thread outright, and it is what resolves the case `decideRoute` otherwise refuses to guess at — a tenant with tenancies at two properties replying about one of them. Lose the key and that message is AMBIGUOUS, and an ambiguous message goes to the unrouted queue. **Which is the same invisible failure D-132 was**: an unrouted message looks exactly like mail from a stranger. Sorting-office mail, autoresponders and anybody whose name a mail client renders as `Last, First` put a comma in that list routinely.

**What it decided.**
- **Not an RFC 5322 parser, and the file says so in as many words.** No groups (`Managers: a@b, c@d;`), no comments, no folded headers, no encoded words. It handles a comma inside a quoted string — including a quoted-pair, so `"O\"Hara, P"` keeps its comma — and a comma inside angle brackets. That is the whole of what breaks on mail people actually send. A real parser is a dependency or a large file, and this header's only job here is to be scanned for one tag.
- **It lives beside `emailAddressOnly`, in core.** D-132's general lesson was that a helper written for one caller, inside the item that needed it, is a helper the next caller does not know exists — which is exactly how the `<…>` unwrap ended up on the recipient half and not the routing half. Both halves of header parsing are now one file.
- **`extractReplyKey` splits again itself**, rather than trusting its caller to have done it. It is the shared function every recipient list reaches, so a caller that hands it a whole unsplit `To:` header now works. Idempotent — a single mailbox splits to itself — so the pre-split path is unchanged.
- **The angle-bracket guard is for malformed input, not legal input.** An addr-spec cannot contain a bare comma, so `<a,b@c>` is already broken; tracking brackets means it costs one unusable recipient rather than two fragments that look like addresses.

**What it left behind.**
- **`emailAddressOnly` still takes the FIRST `<…>` group**, so a display name that itself contains a `<` reads wrongly. Left deliberately: a comma in a display name is the ordinary case, a `<` in one is not, and nothing in the quote-aware split makes that shape newly reachable.
- **Seven unit tests and no new e2e.** The route's `addresses()` is now a two-line flatMap over a tested pure function, and the assertion that actually matters — the key survives a comma'd name beside it — is made against `extractReplyKey` directly.

## R-048 cut — OQ-2 answered, no voucher tenancies
**Commit:** `cb7b09f`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it did.** Re-asked OQ-2 at the point it was actually blocking something, got a firm answer, and cut R-048 rather than leaving it gated. Recorded as **D-136**. No code changed.

**Why it was worth asking rather than deferring again.** OQ-2 was answered "unsure / possible later" on 2026-08-01, and D-13's note said to re-ask before Milestone 3 planning — which never happened, so the row sat gated through five more milestones. It was the **last ungated-by-a-vendor row in the backlog**: R-037a/b, R-093 and R-097b all wait on outside parties, and this one waited on one sentence from the owner. The answer is **none now, none planned**, so the row is cut on D-121's reasoning and R-095/R-096's precedent: a row nobody will build reads to the next reader as work waiting to be done.

**What was cut is the features, not the shape, and that distinction is the whole value of D-13.** Gone are recertification proration on effective dates, one bulk HAP deposit reconciled across many tenant projections, the housing-authority / caseworker / HAP-contract / inspection / abatement records, dunning that never pursues the HAP portion, and failed-HQS auto-work-orders against the re-inspection deadline. **`LeasePayer` and `PayerAllocation` stay**, and they are not dead weight held for a tenant who will not come: an ordinary lease is exactly one `LeasePayer` carrying the whole charge, and allocation always runs, so it is **one code path rather than a special case**. Nothing in the product is paying rent for this cut.

**This is what taking it as a schema decision bought.** D-13 chose the low-regret option in R-002 — build the shape, defer the features — precisely so that whichever way OQ-2 eventually landed, the answer would be cheap. It was. The cut costs nothing to make, and a first voucher tenancy re-opens the row as a **feature build against a schema that already fits**, never as a migration of every financial query. The risk register's Section 8 entry was retired by D-13 in 2026-08-01, **not by this cut**, and that ordering is the thing worth remembering: the architectural risk was closed by a decision made while the answer was still unknown.

**What it left behind.**
- **The backlog now has no ungated row at all.** Every remaining unbuilt item — R-037a, R-037b, R-038a, R-093, R-097b — waits on a vendor relationship or on the furnisher review D-4 already requires. There is no next item to pull without opening one of those gates.
- **Five open questions remain and none of them blocks a build**: OQ-1 (states, 24-month plan), OQ-5 (share of tenants who will never use a portal), OQ-6 (written screening criteria — answered "no" for real use), OQ-8's remaining half (whose books), OQ-10 (after-hours protocol). Each is worth answering for operational reasons; none is a gate.
- **The re-ask itself is the transferable lesson.** OQ-2 carried "re-ask before Milestone 3 planning" and nothing made that happen. A deferred question with no owner and no trigger is a question that gets deferred again — which is the same failure as a checkpoint nobody defines until two milestones later.

## Security review of the unauthenticated surface
**Commit:** `ccc006c`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-24

**What it did.** Swept every entry point that a person with no session can reach, found one real vulnerability, fixed it at its root, and confirmed the rest. Recorded as **D-137**.

**The surface, enumerated rather than assumed.** Seven machine endpoints (`api/cron` ×2, `api/email/inbound`, `api/sms/inbound`, `api/sms/status`, `api/webhooks/resend`, `api/webhooks/stripe`), one token-gated feed (`api/calendar/[token]`), ten token-gated pages (`apply`, `pay`, `prescreen`, `showings`, `showings/access`, `sign`, `vendor`, `vendor/bid`, `verify`, plus the fully public `listings/[id]`), and four routes that hand stored bytes to a browser.

**THE FINDING: stored XSS reachable by a stranger, in the one place four routes each wrote by hand (D-137).**

`Document.contentType` is `file.type` straight off the uploader's `<input type=file>`, and `validateDocument` only ever checked it was non-empty. All four byte-serving routes — `/api/documents/[id]/file`, `/listings/[id]/photos/[documentId]`, `/sign/[token]/document`, `/vendor/[token]/documents/[documentId]` — set `Content-Type: document.contentType` with `Content-Disposition: inline`, none set `nosniff`, and this app serves no CSP.

- **The chain.** An applicant holding an `apply/[token]` link — a stranger who answered a listing — uploads `payslip.svg` declaring `image/svg+xml`. An SVG is not a picture, it is a document that may contain `<script>`. The letting agent opens it to read the payslip, and the attacker's script runs **in this app's origin with that staff member's session attached**. `text/html` is the same attack with less ceremony.
- **Four other ways in.** A tenant's maintenance photo, a tenant's insurance certificate, a vendor's invoice and a staff upload all store `file.type` unexamined.
- **Fixed at the one place bytes meet a browser**, not at the uploads. Guarding the four upload sites leaves the fifth nobody has written yet, and refusing content types at upload would reject real evidence somebody needs to keep — a .docx addendum, an odd camera format. `documentResponse` in `lib/documents/serve.ts` renders an **allowlist of types that cannot execute** inline and serves everything else retyped `application/octet-stream` and dispositioned `attachment`. Nothing is lost but the preview.
- **Retyped as well as dispositioned**, because `attachment` alone still lets a browser reaching the URL another way act on the declared type. And `nosniff` on every response including the renderable path, so a mislabelled `image/png` that is really HTML cannot be sniffed back into the hole.
- **PDF stays inline, deliberately.** It can carry JavaScript, but browsers run it in their own sandboxed viewer rather than the page's origin, and PDF is what this product's whole evidence trail is made of — leases, notices, the eviction packet, the tax archive. Serving those as downloads would break what the product is for, to close a hole the browser already closed.
- **The tell that it was an oversight and not a decision:** the inbound-EMAIL attachment path (R-097d) has exactly the right allowlist, because that item was written knowing a stranger was on the other end. An applicant, a tenant and a vendor are strangers in precisely the same sense. Four hand-written copies of one response is how four routes got it wrong identically — the same shape as D-132 and D-134.

**The first cut of the fix was too strict, and the sweep is what said so.** `text/plain` was not on the allowlist, and a `.txt` proof-of-insurance uploaded on the property page came back as an opaque download — `documents.spec.ts`'s byte-for-byte test went red on both projects. The right answer was to fix the allowlist rather than the test: plain text **cannot** execute, and it is safe here precisely because `nosniff` is set unconditionally, which stops a browser sniffing a `text/plain` body that is really markup and running it as HTML. That is the historic form of this very bug, so the two lines are a pair and the unit test now asserts them together. `text/*` as a class stays off the list — `text/html` and `text/xml` are text too, and both execute.

**What was checked and found sound**, which is worth recording so the next review does not redo it:
- **Token handling is one chokepoint and every caller uses it.** `checkToken` binds purpose, subject type and subject id, is single-use via `consumedAt`, checks purpose and subject *before* expiry so a replay reports the true reason, and all ten consumers pass both `purpose` and `subjectType`. Tokens are 32 CSPRNG bytes stored only as SHA-256.
- **Rate limiting covers every auth flow**: staff login (per IP), MFA verify (keyed on the challenge, not the IP, because six digits is only a million wide), password-reset request and magic-link request. The tenant portal is magic-link only — there is no password path to leave unlimited.
- **Both webhook signatures are constant-time, length-checked and fail closed**, and both are hand-rolled deliberately under D-15's receiver-versus-client distinction.
- **The year-long `CALENDAR_FEED` token's blast-radius claim holds.** Its TTL comment argues safety from "no tenant's name or contact details"; the feed genuinely carries address, unit and event type only, with work-order free text deliberately excluded. Scope is resolved fresh per fetch and `mfaVerified` is always false.
- **`generateStorageKey` cannot traverse** — the filename is sanitised to `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` and prefixed with a UUID — and `storageKey` is only ever read from the row, never from the request.
- **404-not-403 discipline is consistent** across documents, reports and the calendar feed, per ROLE-01.

**What it left behind.**
- **No replay window on the Resend webhook.** Svix signs `${id}.${timestamp}.${body}` and the scheme's timestamp tolerance is what stops a captured request being replayed for ever; this verifier checks the signature and ignores the age. **Not exploitable today** and that was verified rather than assumed: `shouldApplyStatus` is strictly monotonic, so a replayed event cannot walk a delivery backwards or re-fire `flagTenantBounce`, and the endpoint is not wired to a sender at all yet (D-15). Left as a named gap rather than fixed silently, because the file documents Svix's scheme in four numbered steps and omitting the fifth without saying so is the part that will mislead a later reader.
- **No Content-Security-Policy on the app.** The XSS above is closed at its source, but a CSP is the defence that would have contained it, and there is none. That is a deliberate non-goal for this session — it needs its own item, because a CSP added without measuring what the app actually loads is a CSP somebody disables a week later.
- **The confirming sweep had to be run twice, and the first one proved nothing.** It reported 49 failures across fifteen unrelated specs, with tests that normally take about a second taking eight to eighteen minutes each — the environment signature, not a code one. Checked in the order CLAUDE.md prescribes rather than by reading a stack trace: no `JetsamEvent` file for the window (the only one on the machine was nine hours old, so the OS killed nothing), but a leftover 831 MB `next-server` from a previously killed run was still resident, because that cleanup had run the `pkill` line without the `lsof -ti :3100` line beside it. From a verified-clean slate — port free, no residual server, 52% memory available — the same sweep was **998 passed, 8 skipped, 0 flaky in 5.3 minutes**, reconciling exactly against the 1006 listed. A `renewals.spec.ts` failure seen in the bad run did not reproduce either; it had already been measured at 2.1s in isolation against its 60s ceiling, so no timeout was touched on the strength of a run that could not be trusted.
- **No upload-side allowlist**, considered and declined above. If one is ever added it belongs beside `inbound-attachments.ts`'s, not instead of the serve-side guard.

## A nonce-based Content-Security-Policy
**Commit:** `3fa98bd`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it built.** `apps/web/middleware.ts`, a per-request nonce and an enforced CSP on every page, plus `e2e/csp.spec.ts` asserting the header actually exists and says what it should. Recorded as **D-138**.

**The gap D-137 named for itself.** That item closed a stored XSS at its source — uploaded bytes are retyped now — and its own note said a CSP was the defence that *would have contained* it, that there was none, and that one added without measuring is one somebody switches off the first time a page breaks. This is that, done as its own item rather than bolted onto the fix.

**A nonce, not `unsafe-inline`, and that decision is the whole item.** Next's App Router inlines its own hydration and streaming scripts on every page. A policy without a nonce has to allow inline script wholesale — which permits precisely what a CSP exists to stop, and would have made the header decoration. So `middleware.ts` mints a nonce per request and sets the policy on the **request** headers as well as the response: that is how Next finds the nonce to stamp onto its own scripts, and without the request half every page renders script the response header then refuses, i.e. blank.

**Enforced rather than report-only, because there was something better than a report to measure with.** A report-only header collects violations somebody has to go and read. This repo has 1006 e2e tests driving essentially every screen, so turning the real policy on and running the sweep *is* the measurement — and it came back **1006 passed, 8 skipped, 0 flaky against 1014 listed**, the 8 being this item's own.

**What the policy admits, from an inventory rather than a guess.** `js.stripe.com` and `hooks.stripe.com` because `autopay-panel.tsx` is the only third-party script in the product and Elements opens its own iframes — §6.6 keeps card data inside those frames, so `frame-src` is load-bearing. `api.stripe.com` in `connect-src`, which Elements talks to directly. `data:` and `blob:` in `img-src`, because inspection and listing photos are previewed from a local object URL before upload. **No font host at all** — nothing here loads a web font, and an entry for one is a permission granted to something that does not exist.

**What it decided.**
- **The matcher excludes `/api/` and the three non-api routes that serve document bytes**, and that exclusion is the sharpest thing in the item. `documentResponse` answers `default-src 'none'; sandbox` for any type it will not render; a blanket page policy applied there would have **replaced it with a weaker one — the middleware silently undoing the D-137 fix it was written to back up**. `csp.spec.ts` asserts the exclusion holds, because a matcher regex with one character wrong protects nothing while every other test in the suite stays green.
- **`style-src` keeps `'unsafe-inline'`**, a bounded concession rather than an oversight. React and Stripe both set inline styles, nonce-ing every one is a large change to component code, and inline *style* cannot execute script — the worst it buys an attacker is defacement, against a `script-src` that still refuses to run anything.
- **`'strict-dynamic'` is paired with the Stripe host, not used instead of it.** A browser that understands it ignores host allowlists and trusts what an already-trusted script loads, which is exactly how Stripe.js and Next's own chunks arrive; an older browser falls back to the host entry.
- **`frame-ancestors`, `base-uri`, `form-action` and `object-src` are all locked**, one line each. An injected `<base>` silently repoints every relative URL including the ones forms post to, and clickjacking a page that ends a tenancy is worth the line.

**What it left behind.**
- **A per-request nonce means a page carrying one cannot be statically generated.** Nearly every page here is behind a session and already dynamic, so the loss is small — but it is real, and a future item that wants a page prerendered has to reckon with this file. Named in the middleware's own header rather than discovered later.
- **`style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is the one soft spot** and could be closed by nonce-ing component styles. Not worth it against the current threat model; if it is ever done, it is a component-wide change, not a header edit.
- **Nothing verifies the policy against a real browser console.** The suite proves pages work and the header is right; it does not prove no resource is being silently blocked in a way no assertion notices. A blocked request that nothing asserts on would pass here.

## The CSP was switching off the JavaScript on four pages
**Commit:** `dcb8e75`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it did.** Built the browser-behaviour check D-138 said was missing, and it immediately found that D-138 itself had broken four pages. Recorded as **D-139**.

**D-138 shipped green and wrong.** Its own "what it left behind" said the suite proved pages work and the header is correct, and that nothing proved no resource was being silently blocked. That was the exact defect sitting in it: `/`, `/forgot-password`, `/login/mfa` and `/portal/login` were serving **fourteen script tags each, every one refused by the browser**. The full sweep passed anyway — 1006 tests, zero failures.

**Why it was invisible, and it is a compliment to the codebase.** CLAUDE.md's standing rule is that anything which must work on first paint is a real `<form action>` plus `useActionState`, never a button with an `onClick`. Because the product obeys that, all four pages kept working with their JavaScript entirely dead — sign-in, the MFA challenge, the tenant magic link and password reset all still functioned server-side. **A codebase that degraded worse would have failed loudly.**

**The mechanism, measured rather than reasoned about.** The nonce is minted per request; statically prerendered HTML is fixed at build time, so there is no request for it to come from and Next stamps none. `'strict-dynamic'` then makes `'self'` inert, so nothing was left to allow the chunks. Confirmed by counting script tags against the running production build:

| page | render mode | script tags | carrying a nonce |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/login` | dynamic | 14 | **14** |
| `/` | prerendered | 14 | **0** |

The prerender manifest named exactly seven routes, four of them real pages. Those four now carry `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, with the reason written beside each one.

**What it decided.**
- **`'strict-dynamic'` is kept, and the tempting conclusion — that it was too strict — is backwards.** It is what made a page with no nonce fail *completely* rather than partially, which is the only reason this was findable at all. Without it those pages would have loaded their chunks via `'self'` and lost only the inline hydration payload: a subtler breakage, in a suite that already could not see the loud one.
- **The detector leads with a negative control**, because an empty violation list is equally the result of a correct policy and of a listener that was never registered — CLAUDE.md's most-repeated trap, and one this file would have walked straight into. `csp-browser.spec.ts` first makes the browser refuse an injected inline event handler and asserts both that it did not execute *and* that the detector saw it. That test is also the only thing in the repo proving the CSP stops a real injection rather than describing one.
- **The payload is markup, not a DOM-API script.** The first negative control used `createElement('script')` + `textContent` and **failed — it executed.** That is `'strict-dynamic'` working as specified: trust propagates to what a trusted script loads, and an attacker who can already run script has nothing left to bypass. The injection a CSP defends against arrives as markup the parser inserts, so the test now uses an inline `onerror` handler. Written down next to the test so nobody "fixes" it back.
- **`securitypolicyviolation` events, not console scraping.** A console filter has to match wording that varies by browser and version, and cannot tell a CSP refusal from any other red line.

**What it left behind.**
- **`/_not-found` and `/_global-error` are still prerendered**, so their scripts are still refused. Left deliberately: both are static error pages with no interactivity, and forcing framework error boundaries dynamic is a change with more risk than the defect it would fix. Named here so it is a decision rather than an oversight.
- **A newly-added static page would reintroduce this silently.** The spec names the four routes the manifest listed rather than reading the manifest at runtime; a fifth prerendered page would not be covered. Reading `prerender-manifest.json` from the spec would close it and couples the suite to a Next internal — worth doing if it ever happens twice.
- **Stripe is still unexercised in the browser.** `autopay-panel.tsx` is the only third-party script and D-15 already excludes it from e2e, so `js.stripe.com`, `hooks.stripe.com` and `api.stripe.com` are admitted by the policy on inventory rather than on a passing test.

## The prerender guard D-139 left behind
**Commit:** `543d515`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it did.** Closed the one gap D-139 named: its tests watched the four routes already known to be broken, so a *fifth* prerendered page added later would have reintroduced the defect silently. No new decision — this is the guard that item said was missing.

**A build-time allowlist rather than a runtime check, which is the reversal.** D-139's note said this was worth doing "if it ever happens twice", because the version being declined read the prerender manifest at runtime and coupled the suite to a Next internal. The cheaper shape is to assert the manifest's route set equals an **accepted set**: `/_not-found`, `/_global-error` and `/manifest.webmanifest`, each a framework page with no interactivity. Anything else failing the check is a page that will lose every script, and the failure message says so and names the fix. It encodes the decision instead of re-testing the behaviour.

**Proved in both directions, because a guard that cannot fail is the mistake this whole thread was about.** `/forgot-password` was temporarily reverted to static and the suite rebuilt: the guard failed and named it, and — independently — the behavioural test reported **66 blocked resources** on that page. Restored, and 18 CSP tests pass. Without that second run the guard would have been another assertion that is always true, which is the trap CLAUDE.md says has now been hit four times.

**What it left behind.** The accepted set is a literal. If Next ever renames its internal routes the check fails loudly and correctly, which is the right direction for a guard to fail in.

## R-038a: offline part-payments, and the shipped bug the probe found
**Commit:** `b7a58ce`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it built.** Offline part-payments (PAY-05's last refusal), and — found on the way to them — the fix for a money bug that had been live since R-038. Recorded as **D-141** (the projection change) and **D-142** (the offline change), two decisions because they are two different things that happen to share one fix.

**The gate the row named was met, and the row was right to insist on it.** R-038a was gated on "a test Stripe key", because the mechanics turn on invoice/balance interactions the simulator cannot reproduce and D-15 forbids guessing at. A key was in `.env.local`, so the item opened with a probe against the real test account rather than a design.

**The route the backlog proposed does not work, and that was measured rather than argued.** Credit $500 to the customer against an open $1000 invoice and `amount_remaining` stays `100000`. The credit parks on the customer and waits for the *next* finalization — so a tenant who paid half at the counter would go on being dunned for the whole thing. The row suspected this ("note 'next', which is the wrinkle"); the probe settled it.

**What works is `attach_payment`.** Report a `PaymentRecord` (`processor_details[type]=custom`, `outcome=guaranteed` in the same call rather than a second round trip, because PAY-05's fifteen seconds is a real budget) and attach it to the invoice. Measured: 50000 against a 100000 invoice leaves it `open` with `amount_remaining` 50000 and nothing written off; attaching the rest closes it to `paid`. Works at the pinned `2024-06-20`, so no API-version change was needed — which was worth checking before designing around one.

**Then the thing nobody was looking for.** Establishing which webhooks a partial attach fires meant enumerating every event Stripe emits per payment path. For an invoice paid the way R-038 pays it:

```
invoice.created → invoice.updated → invoice.finalized → invoice.updated → invoice.paid
```

Five events, and **`invoice.payment_succeeded` is not one of them — Stripe does not send it for `paid_out_of_band`.** The live endpoint subscribed to ten types; neither `invoice.paid` nor `invoice.updated` was among them, and neither was in `HANDLED_EVENTS`. So **every check, money order and cash payment ever recorded through R-038 pushed to Stripe correctly, wrote our `Payment` row, and never produced a `LedgerEntry`.** The charge posted at `invoice.finalized` stayed on the books; the tenant's balance never moved. Under D-11 that projection is what dunning, late fees, the rent roll and every notice read.

**Why nothing caught it, which is the more useful half.** The simulator's `markInvoicePaidOutOfBand` was a `console.info`. It emitted no event, so against the simulator the ledger did not move either — and the test that would have failed was never written, because there was nothing to assert. This is not D-27's "the simulator agrees with us by construction"; it is the quieter version, **a simulator that skips the consequence entirely**, which leaves a hole shaped exactly like the consequence. The fix makes the simulator drive the same `processStripeEvent` the webhook route drives.

**One rule fixes both, and that is why they are one item.** `invoice.updated` fires with `previous_attributes.amount_paid` on **every** money path — out-of-band, card, and a partial attach, all three measured — and carries the exact delta:

```
partial attach:  0     → 50000    (delta 50000, invoice still open)
closing attach:  50000 → 100000   (delta 50000, invoice paid)
card payment:    0     → 100000   (delta 100000)
out-of-band:     0     → 100000   (delta 100000)
```

So money in is projected from that delta and `invoice.payment_succeeded` is no longer handled. It is a strict superset of the old signal, so this is one event replacing one event rather than a second one added — and adding rather than replacing would have credited every card payment twice.

**What it decided.**
- **The delta, never the total, and `previous_attributes` is why the interpreter stays pure.** `amount_paid` is cumulative: the instalment that closes a 100000 invoice reports 100000 having moved 50000. Projecting the reported figure would credit 150000 against a 100000 bill, into an append-only ledger where the only correction is a reversing entry somebody first has to notice is needed. Stripe puts the previous value on the event, so no database read is needed to subtract.
- **The `previous_attributes.amount_paid` guard is what makes a high-volume event safe to handle.** An `invoice.updated` for finalization, a metadata edit or a rendering change does not list `amount_paid` as changed, and is ignored with a stated reason. The accepted cost: a `ProcessedStripeEvent` row per invoice edit. Deliberate — the alternative is a filter that has to be right about which edits matter.
- **A negative delta is ignored.** Money going the other way is a refund or a reversal, and those arrive as their own events with their own linkage; projecting it here would post a second, unlinked correction on top of the real one.
- **The webhook subscription was changed in the same breath as the code.** The code alone is inert: `invoice.updated` was not on the endpoint. Both halves are now in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` with the reason attached, because swapping them back would silently reintroduce the bug.
- **Idempotency is load-bearing here in a way it was not for R-038.** The old call was protected by Stripe simply refusing to pay a paid invoice. A partial has no equivalent state, so a retried submission would be money the tenant never handed over. The key is on the FACT — payer, day, channel, check number, amount — so a retry reports the same `PaymentRecord`, and Stripe then refuses to attach that record twice. Both halves were tested against the real API.
- **`blockPartialPayments` is checked at the counter, and it belongs to this item.** R-038 could not take a part-payment at all, so PAY-12's switch was satisfied by accident. Making them possible without checking it would reopen exactly the hazard the switch exists for: in many states accepting a partial after serving notice can void the eviction, and the counter is where that happens. Checked against the BALANCE, not the open invoice, because the switch's own words are "the full balance or nothing".
- **The refusal was swapped, not removed.** `partial_not_supported` became `more_than_invoiced` — less is fine now, more is not, and Stripe itself refuses to attach a payment larger than the remainder (measured). A raw Stripe error at the counter is not a message anybody can act on.

**What it left behind.**
- **The payments already recorded with no ledger entry behind them are reported, not backfilled.** Owner's call, and the right one: a corrective write across historical money records has a larger blast radius than the fix itself and deserves its own item and an explicit go.
- **Reconciliation cannot see this bug's shape, and now says so.** R-035 compares the projection against our own processed-event log. An event Stripe *never sent* leaves nothing on either side — no processed event missing a row, no row missing an event. Both sides agreed because both were empty. What would catch it is walking Stripe's own invoices for the window and comparing each `amount_paid` against the projection; that is external reconciliation done properly and belongs to its own item. Named in `reconcile.ts` rather than left to be discovered a second time.
- **`certifiedFundsOnly` is still unchecked on the offline path.** Pre-existing — it predates this item and is not created by it — and deliberately not fixed while fixing something else: whether a personal check, a money order or cash counts as certified funds is a legal question for the review D-4 already requires.
- **The simulator's emission is synchronous, and production's is not.** In production the projection lands after the action returns; here it has already landed. A caller reading the balance immediately after recording would look correct in tests and race in production. Stated in the simulator rather than left as a trap.
- **The account's default API version is `2026-07-29.dahlia` while the adapter pins `2024-06-20`.** The webhook endpoint inherits the account default, and under dahlia the invoice object has no `payment_intent` field — so `stripePaymentIntentId` is already always null on projected invoice payments. Not a defect, but it is a mismatch nobody had written down, and it is the kind that makes a future field read return null for reasons that look like a bug.

## R-100a: the maintenance and vendor story, and a reset that survives it
**Commit:** `28441eb`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it built.** The demo seed's operational half (PRD §8, D-140's first slice) and the `--reset` rewrite that seeding it forced. Recorded as **D-143**.

**The story, keyed by unit.** `MAINTENANCE` is a map from `"<property>::<unit>"` to a plan, merged into `buildPlan()` rather than nested inside the property literal — the literal was already two hundred lines, and a key that names its property and unit in words fails loudly when a unit is renamed where a nested field would silently move with it. What it seeds:

- **An emergency nobody has picked up** — a habitability-flagged leak, `firstResponseAt` deliberately null and never acknowledged. The escalation ladder and the emergency queue have nothing to show unless a page is genuinely outstanding, and this is the single most demo-worthy row in the file.
- **A ticket waiting on the tenant** mid-conversation, which is what a triage queue is mostly made of and what a screenshot never shows.
- **A job booked and confirmed**, with the vendor's acceptance and a future window, so the calendar and the entry-notice path render.
- **A vendor mid-dispatch with one live magic link**, dispatched yesterday and unanswered — what the no-response timer measures. The raw token is printed once at the end of the run and is unrecoverable afterwards, because only its SHA-256 is stored.
- **A completed turn** with the vendor's bill already in, an inspection due with unanswered items, one performed and locked, three vendors (one deliberately without a W-9, so the payment-blocked path is reachable), and three preventive schedules.

Eight messages ride on real `Thread` rows keyed with core's own `threadKey` rather than a string built in the seed — a seed that invented its own key format would produce threads production's routing cannot find, which is a demo conversation no inbound reply would ever land in.

**Staff are found, never created.** `db:create-owner` owns making an account and should stay the only thing that does. The seed refuses with that command in the error rather than seeding around it: every work order, inspection and staff reply has to be attributable to somebody, and a demo you cannot log into is not a demo.

**The reset was the real work, exactly as the row predicted.** `Message` is append-only by trigger, and `Message.ticketId`/`workOrderId` are `onDelete: Restrict` deliberately — a `SET NULL` cascade is an UPDATE the trigger rejects. So the old bottom-up delete now throws *partway*, after the charges, leases and tenants above the tickets are already gone. **A half-deleted demo is worse than either outcome**, which is why the decision moved up to the property: deleted whole or retired whole, and the two branches never mix. Sticky means any `AuditLog` row or any `Thread` holding messages.

**What it decided.**
- **Retiring means deactivated AND renamed, and the rename is the half that is easy to skip.** `reset()` finds what it owns by name. A retired vendor left holding its original name is found again by the next reset, which tries to delete it and is refused by the retired property's work orders still pointing at it. Caught by running three consecutive resets rather than one — the first reset passes either way.
- **Retiring a work order revokes its vendor link.** Without it, every reset left another unexpired `VENDOR_WORK_ORDER` token pointing at a retired job — a live credential to a gate code nobody would ever think to revoke. Measured before and after: four live tokens accumulating, versus one held steady across three resets.
- **Retired rows accumulate, three properties per reset, and that is correct.** The evidence trail deliberately outlives the entity it describes. The console line says how many were retired and why, so it reads as a decision rather than a leak.
- **The open-status list moved to core.** It had two readers and one copy, and the second reader could not see it — see the defect below.

**The defect this item found in itself.** The turn was first seeded as `INVOICED`, which is **not** in the list `listOpenWorkOrders` filters on — the work orders page says so in its own comment — so the finished job was invisible on the only screen that renders work orders. That is R-036b's lesson in its purest form, and the sibling row R-100b warns about it in exactly these words: a status existing in the enum, and in the write that sets it, says nothing about the lists that READ it. Fixed twice over: the status became `WORK_COMPLETE` (which is what R-100a asked for anyway, still carries the invoice, and still feeds the spend report), and the list moved to `packages/core/workorders` as `OPEN_WORK_ORDER_STATUSES` so that the query and a test now read the same one.

**What it was verified against.** A throwaway local database, created and dropped for the purpose — **not** `.env.local`, which points at a Neon cloud branch, and not the shared test database, whose e2e locators the seed's own header warns about colliding with. From a clean database: seed, then three consecutive resets, ending at six active properties, three active vendors, five active tenants and exactly one live vendor token every time. `demo-seed.test.ts` adds six pure assertions over the plan data — the two that matter are that no seeded status is one the screens filter out, and that every `"<property>::<unit>"` key names a unit that exists. Both were confirmed to fail when the defect they describe is reintroduced.

**What it left behind.**
- **`Task` rows are not seeded.** R-100a's row does not ask for them and D-9's one queue deserves its own thought about which tasks a demo should open with, rather than a handful invented here.
- **The Neon dev branch cannot be migrated.** `prisma migrate deploy` against `.env.local` answers `P3005` — the schema is not empty and has no migration history, so it has never been baselined. Nothing in this item touched it and nothing in this item depends on it, but `db:migrate:dev` and `db:status:dev` exist precisely so this cannot go unnoticed, and right now they cannot succeed. It needs a deliberate baseline decision, which is not a thing to do as a side effect of a seed change.
- **Nobody has walked these screens in a browser.** The statuses are asserted against the lists that filter them and the seed runs clean, which is stronger than it was — but D-28's demo-checkpoint discipline is a walk, and this item did not do one. R-100b and R-100c both land on the same screens; the walk belongs after the last of them, not three times over.
- **The seed still writes no `AuditLog`.** Matching `seed.mts`'s reference rows, and consistent with these not being real user actions. It means the audit trail on a freshly seeded demo is empty, which is a gap somebody will notice on the evidence-trail screens.

## R-100b: the leasing and risk story
**Commit:** `a772cbf`  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it built.** The demo seed's second slice (PRD §8, D-140), following R-100a's shape exactly: a `LEASING` map keyed `"<property>::<unit>"`, merged in after the units it hangs off exist. Recorded as **D-144**.

- **The vacancy, end to end** on Magnolia's ADU: a PUBLISHED listing with three photos, six prospects at every stage from INQUIRY to APPROVED, applications written only for those past APPLIED, and a lease already out for signature on the one who got approved — `PENDING_SIGNATURE` behind a `PARTIALLY_SIGNED` envelope with one signer done and one still out.
- **The tenant who is behind**, on the unit `buildPlan()` already marks `late` with an overdue charge — so the notice and the eviction case land on somebody the rest of the demo already shows as late, rather than on a tenant who looks current everywhere else. Served three days ago with a three-day cure, and the case held at `NOTICE`: nothing filed, the clock still running.
- **The fair-housing pair**, and the most instructive thing in the seed: an unauthorized-animal case answered by an assistance-animal request nobody has decided yet — which is precisely when that decision is still being made correctly or incorrectly.
- **Compliance**, one overdue and two upcoming. All green demonstrates nothing; all red looks like a broken seed rather than a portfolio.

**The row's warning paid off, and only twice.** "Every status enum is a trap here" — but reading the queries showed only two actually filter, and both are now asserted rather than remembered: the public listing page is `where: { status: 'PUBLISHED' }`, so a DRAFT listing is not a quieter demo but a 404; and the violation page's accommodation panel filters to `RECEIVED`/`INFO_REQUESTED`, so an approved request would be seeded onto a case from which nobody can reach it. Everything else — notices, evictions, violations, compliance, prospects — lists whatever is in scope.

**Two reset bugs, both found by counting rather than by crashing.**

**One: proof of service is append-only.** `NoticeDelivery` carries a `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger and `NoticeDelivery.noticeId` is `onDelete: Restrict`, so a served notice can never be deleted, and neither can the notice or the lease under it. D-143 predicted this maintenance burden and guessed the wrong table — it expected `Notification` to be next. Worth recording precisely: **there are six append-only tables, not the four CLAUDE.md lists** — `AuditLog`, `LedgerEntry`, `Message`, `Notification`, plus `NoticeDelivery` and `TenantConsent`.

**Two: compliance items leaked three per run.** Every other count held steady across resets and this one went 3, 6, 9 — an entity-scoped item has `propertyId: null` and matched no property-keyed delete at all. Fixing that surfaced a second bug immediately: `ComplianceItem` has a check constraint that exactly one of `propertyId`/`legalEntityId` is set, so the `SET NULL` a property delete cascades makes the row illegal and the *property* delete fails. Same shape as the `JobRun` unique-key collision this file already documents, same fix — delete it before the property, not after — and the same misleading symptom, since the error is reported against a table the caller was not writing.

**What it decided.**
- **Compliance items are deleted unconditionally, on both branches.** They are the only rows here carrying no evidence: the seed writes them uncompleted, so there is no completion, no document, no proof — just a due date somebody invented. That is what makes them safe to delete where nothing else is.
- **A tenant and a lease are created for the envelope rather than promoted from the approved prospect.** Promotion is a real flow with its own screens (R-063), and a seed that half-performs it would leave a prospect in a state the real flow never produces.
