- **The violation's narrative is an observation, not a column.** `ViolationCase` has no summary field, and that is the schema saying something worth listening to: what somebody saw, on a stated day, recorded by a named person, is evidence. A case carrying free text and no observation is an allegation with nobody behind it.
- **Lease templates are found, never written** — the same posture as staff. A `LEASE` envelope has a database check constraint requiring a template, and a demo seed inventing lease text is a demo seed with an opinion about a legal document. It refuses with `npm run db:seed:lease-templates` in the message.
- **Photos are placeholder tiles, and skipped entirely when storage is remote.** Three 1×1 PNGs written to local disk; `object-cover` renders them as clean solid blocks. When `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN` is set they are skipped with a console line saying so, because rows whose bytes do not exist render as broken images — worse than a listing with none — and this script has no business writing to a shared blob store.

**What it was verified against.** A throwaway local database again, created and dropped: seed, then **four** consecutive resets, with every count steady at the end — six active properties, three vendors, six tenants, one published listing, six prospects, three photos, one served notice, one undecided accommodation, one live vendor token, three compliance items. `demo-seed.test.ts` grew from six assertions to sixteen. Nothing in `apps/web` changed, so the e2e suite is untouched by this item.

**What it left behind.**
- **`ListingSyndication` is not seeded**, so the syndication screen still opens empty. R-100b's row does not ask for it and a fake feed status against a simulated adapter would be a screen that lies rather than one that is blank.
- **No screening report or decision.** "Applications at each screening stage" was read as the funnel stage on `Prospect`, which is where that status actually lives — `Application` has none. A seeded adverse-action decision is a heavier thing than it looks (R-060's criteria versioning and order-of-application processing) and belongs with whoever demos screening properly.
- **The `.data/documents` bytes are left behind by `--reset`.** The Document rows go; the files stay. A seed script deleting files by a path it reconstructed itself is a worse bug than a few stale kilobytes, and they are 70 bytes each.
- **Still nobody has walked these screens in a browser.** Unchanged from R-100a and deliberately so: R-100c lands on the same screens, and the walk belongs after it rather than three times over.

## R-100c: the money story, replayed rather than seeded
**Commit:** fab46252eba3c7b56b05741aa4e69e495316b9b5  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**What it built.** The demo seed's third and last slice (PRD §8, D-11, D-145) — and the only one that writes no money rows of its own. D-11 makes `LedgerEntry` an append-only projection of Stripe, so balances, payment history, autopay state and a tenancy mid-chase were never a seeding problem: they are a *replay* problem. `seedMoney()` builds Stripe event envelopes and pushes them through `processStripeEvent`, the same function the live webhook route calls, and every ledger row, `Payment`, receipt and failed-payment notice in the demo comes out of that pipeline. The route was D-145's open choice and is recorded as **D-146**.

- **Five tenancies, one per lifecycle**, keyed on the `lifecycle` string `buildPlan()` already carries rather than on a second `"<property>::<unit>"` map. Between them they reach every path the pipeline has: **square on autopay** (Maria), **mid-chase** — two clean months then an invoice declined and never paid, carrying the overdue `Charge` the plan already seeded (Derrick, who R-100b already hung the notice and the eviction case on), **a part-payment on `send_invoice`** leaving $200 of $1,600 owed (Priya), **an ACH still in flight** — a PENDING `Payment` and no ledger movement at all (Wanda), and **a decline then a successful retry** (Grant).
- **`LeasePayer` rows and the Stripe customers behind them**, which D-145 noted this item owned. Through `provisionLeaseBilling` — the product's own path — so with `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` set these are genuine test-mode customers and subscriptions.
- **`reset()` gained two sticky sources, a subscription cancellation and a listing unpublish.** Details below.

**Why `tsx` and a resolve hook (D-146).** `processStripeEvent` is `server-only` and reaches the app through `@/`; neither resolves in a plain node script. D-145 left three routes open. Route (a) — POSTing signed bodies to the running app — was rejected not mainly for needing a server and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, but because **the simulated provider's state is per process**: customers created by this script live in this script's `SimulatedBillingProvider`, so an autopay enrolment handled inside the app would be asking a simulator that had never heard of them. Route (c) is a twelve-line `module.registerHooks` resolver pointing `server-only` at the same empty stub `vitest.config.ts` already uses. **Bare `node` still could not run it** — strip-only TypeScript refuses a constructor parameter property in the screening simulator — hence `tsx`, already a devDependency, and `db:seed:demo` now runs under it.

**What is real and what is authored, stated plainly.** The customers and subscriptions are real. The events are not, and cannot be: a demo needs three months of rent history on the day it is seeded, and Stripe would take three months to emit it. D-145's own route (a) already assumed authored bodies — "POST signed event bodies" is the same envelope with an HTTP hop in front — so this is not a narrowing of the decision, but it is worth saying out loud rather than leaving a reader to infer it.

**The bug the real Stripe account found, which the simulator never would.** The first version invented a `pm_...` id for the autopay enrolment. Against `.env.local`'s test key Stripe refused it outright — *No such PaymentMethod* — and the seed stopped, correctly, because `seedMoney` states the expected outcome at every call site. `savedPaymentMethod()` now does the one thing this script stands in for a browser to do: creates a real SetupIntent through the adapter and confirms it with Stripe's own `pm_card_visa`, guarded on `sk_test_`. **The assertion is the reason this was found rather than shipped**: `enrolAutopay` catches its own failures by design, so without a stated expectation the seed would have reported success over a demo where autopay was silently off — the D-132 failure shape exactly, where the broken thing looks like the thing working.

**Three reset bugs' worth of maintenance, found by counting.**

**One: two more sticky sources, and `Notification` is not redundant.** `LedgerEntry` is the strongest yet — deleting a demo property that has ever been billed would manufacture the reconciliation bug D-11 exists to prevent. `Notification` looks subsumed by it and is not: a payment **failure** writes a `payment.failed_fix` notification and **no ledger entry at all**, because nothing has changed about what is owed. A tenancy whose only money event was a decline is notified and unbilled. **That is the fifth sticky source in three items** — treat the set as something that grows, and note that there are **six append-only tables, not the four CLAUDE.md lists**.

**Two: a retired tenancy kept its subscription.** Same shape as R-100a's vendor tokens, one rung more serious: a retired demo lease still holding a live subscription goes on raising invoices, and every reset would add five more. Cancelled through the provider rather than by clearing the id — clearing it would leave the subscription running with nothing pointing at it, an orphan our own reconciliation could no longer name.

**Three: a publicly reachable listing, and this one was caused by this item.** Making Magnolia's tenancy billable made the whole property sticky, and it had been on the deletable branch before. Its listing therefore survived — and `listingForPublic` is `where: { id, status: 'PUBLISHED' }` with **no scope and no active check**, while every internal screen had correctly forgotten it because `currentScope` filters on `property.active`. The retired property's listings are now unpublished. The rest of its leasing rows (six prospects a run) are left alone deliberately: they are invisible to every screen for exactly the `currentScope` reason, and unpicking a retired property from the bottom is the thing this function's own header forbids.

**What it decided.**
- **Keyed by lifecycle, not by unit.** `MAINTENANCE` and `LEASING` hang off a place; money hangs off a *tenancy*, and `lifecycle` is already the word for what kind of tenancy each one is. A second key saying the same thing is a second thing to keep in sync.
- **Cents, never a fraction of the rent.** `paidCents` is an explicit array of amounts. A fraction of a money amount is a rounding bug waiting to be found.
- **The part month at move-in is billed and paid, not left hanging.** `chargeMoveInProration` runs inside provisioning (R-042) and leaves a real `Charge` with nothing on the ledger — so without an invoice for it, every demo tenancy would carry a part-month rent charge showing as fully outstanding for ever on the pay screen. Billed and paid on the day the tenancy started, because that is when it happened.
- **The `send_invoice` payer is created *before* provisioning.** `provisionLeaseBilling` creates the subscription with whatever collection method the payer row already carries (D-29). Switching afterwards is R-047's guarded flow — which would refuse this payer anyway, because they have an open invoice, which is the guard working.
- **`seedMoney` states the expected outcome of every replay and throws otherwise.** Every failure mode here is silent: an unknown customer is `ignored` with a reason, a replayed id is a `duplicate`, and both leave the seed reporting success over an empty rent roll.
- **`ProcessedStripeEvent` rows are never deleted by `--reset`**, unchanged from R-035's reasoning: a cleanup that removed them once left real ledger orphans behind.

**What it was verified against.** A throwaway local database, created and dropped, against the **real Stripe test-mode account** in `.env.local`: seed, then **four** consecutive resets, with every count scoped to active properties identical at each of the five checkpoints — six properties, six tenants, three vendors, five billed payers, one published listing, six prospects, three compliance items, one live vendor token, 38 ledger entries, 22 payments, two tenancies owing, one payment pending, one payer on autopay. Balances land exactly where the plan says: $0, $1,650 owed, $200 owed, $0 with $1,950 uncredited in flight, $0. `demo-seed.test.ts` grew from 16 assertions to 26. **Nothing in `apps/web` changed**, so the e2e suite is untouched by this item; `lint`, `typecheck` and the full 2,711-test unit suite are green.

**What it left behind.**
- **Test-mode customers accumulate in the Stripe account.** `--reset` cancels their subscriptions, which is the part that would otherwise keep billing, but the customers themselves stay. Deleting a Stripe customer from a seed script is a bigger hammer than the mess justifies; clearing them out is a dashboard job.
- **No refund, dispute or ACH return in the demo.** All three are handled paths (`charge.refunded`, `charge.dispute.created`, and the return that reverses a settled payment), and none is seeded. A return in particular is a *reversal* of money that already settled, which would make the demo's mid-chase story ambiguous — the tenant who is behind should be behind for one legible reason.
- **The demo tenancies bill on the 1st and their invoices are dated in relative days**, not on calendar month boundaries. Every date in this seed is relative so it stays current months later; the cost is that a statement reads "30 days ago" rather than "1 August".
- **Still nobody has walked these screens in a browser.** Unchanged from R-100a and R-100b, and now the thing to do next: all three slices are in, and the demo checkpoint walk (D-28) is what has caught every status-enum trap this build has found.

## R-104: wire real email and SMS
**Commits:** 88f00e09e47d498e9c5fc587b40759330893f164, bf69e16c8ca8628860335f13db64c7aed1bade58  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**Renumbered before it landed.** The Milestone 10 row was written as R-101, which R-101 (the live-region fix) has owned since it shipped - along with R-101b/c/d and R-102/R-103. The row took the sequence number for its ID without checking. It is **R-104** everywhere.

**What it built.** The two provider drivers D-15 left as a seam, spent exactly as D-15 said they would be: `apps/web/lib/notifications/live-adapter.ts`, and one changed assignment in `provider.ts`. Nothing else in the product moved. Every module already routes through the engine (R-030), the engine already routes through `deliverOverChannel`, and that already routes through `notificationAdapter` — so wiring Resend and Twilio touched one line of wiring and no caller.

- **Resend**, a JSON POST to `api.resend.com/emails` carrying `from`, `to`, `subject`, `text` and — when the message belongs to a thread — `reply_to`. Returns Resend's `id`, which is what the R-054 bounce webhook matches deliveries on.
- **Twilio**, a form POST to `api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/<sid>/Messages.json` through the messaging service, with basic auth. Returns the `sid`.
- **`fetch`, not SDKs** (D-147). Each provider is one documented request with one documented error shape; `resend` and `twilio` would have added two dependency trees and two release cadences to save about fifteen lines each.
- **Every SMS now carries `StatusCallback={AUTH_URL}/api/sms/status`.** R-040e built that route and said in its own header that nothing could reach it while the logging adapter was wired. This is the line that reaches it, and it is what lets `SENT` stop meaning merely *the provider accepted it* for `entry_notice` (D-38).

**The decision that took the thinking: what an unconfigured provider does.** There is no Resend key on this laptop and none in CI, and there never will be — so a driver that simply replaced the logging adapter would have turned every notification in the 596-test suite into `unsupported_channel` and told the truth about nothing. The driver therefore **delegates to `LoggingChannelAdapter` when a provider's variables are absent**, which keeps a laptop and CI behaving exactly as they did before this item.

That fallback is a lie on a real deployment, and the lie is the specific one this engine exists to prevent: `SENT` on a delivery row for a message that reached nobody. So **on a production deployment the fallback is refused** — `supports()` answers false for the unconfigured channel and the engine records SUPPRESSED / `unsupported_channel`, which is a path it was already written for, per-channel, so a missing SMS provider still lets the email go out.

**`VERCEL_ENV`, never `NODE_ENV`, and this is the trap worth writing down.** The e2e suite runs a **production build** (R-042), so `NODE_ENV === 'production'` is true on a laptop holding no keys at all. Keyed off `NODE_ENV`, the production guard would have switched off every notification in the local sweep — the failure looking exactly like the feature working, which is the D-132 shape again. `VERCEL_ENV=production` is set only on the real deployment.

**What it decided.**
- **Text-only email.** Every template in `packages/core/notifications/templates.ts` renders plain text. An HTML body built by wrapping that text in tags is a new and untested rendering of wording that is sometimes legally significant.
- **A thread reply gets a default subject.** `sendThreadMessage` passes no subject at all — SMS has no such field and `Thread` has no subject column — and Resend requires one. A constant beats inventing a subject from the body.
- **An accepted send with no id is a failure, not a success.** Both drivers throw `ChannelSendError` when the provider returns 2xx without an `id`/`sid`. A delivery row with no external id can never be reconciled by either webhook, so recording it as SENT would be recording something unverifiable.
- **The providers' own codes are the failure codes.** Resend's `name` (`validation_error`, `rate_limit_exceeded`) and Twilio's numeric `code`. The numeric one matters twice over: `isOptOutErrorCode` in `packages/core/comms` already reads exactly those on the status callback, so a STOP'd recipient records the same `21610` whichever path found it.
- **Both providers answer 4xx with JSON rather than throwing**, so `response.ok` is the whole difference between a recorded rejection and a silent success with no id. That is what most of the new test file is about.

**The third instance of a hazard this repo has already met twice, caught before the keys arrived rather than after.** `LiveChannelAdapter` selects a real provider on the presence of its variables — exactly as `getBillingProvider()` selects Stripe on `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and the storage seam selects Blob on `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN`. Both of those are emptied in `vitest.config.ts` and `playwright.config.ts` precisely because `.env.local` is loaded by the test scripts, and this one is worse than either: the moment a Resend key landed in `.env.local`, **the suites would have sent real email and real SMS — hundreds of them**, to whatever `NOTIFICATIONS_SANDBOX_TO` named, or to the fixture's invented address when it named nothing. `RESEND_API_KEY`, `TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID`, `TWILIO_MESSAGING_SERVICE_SID` and `NOTIFICATIONS_SANDBOX_TO` are now emptied in both runners. **`TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN` is deliberately left alone** — it verifies the signature on the *inbound* webhook (R-021) and the suite needs it — and emptying the other two Twilio values is enough, because the driver requires all three. The sandbox variable goes too, for a second reason: it rewrites the recipient the log records, and specs assert on that address. **Verified by probe rather than by reasoning**, which is the only way to know a runner's `env` block beats a real shell variable: with all four set to plausible values in the environment, the notification tests still logged `EMAIL -> ops@example.test` — the logging adapter, and the un-redirected address.

**What it was verified against.** `live-adapter.test.ts`, eight tests over a stubbed `fetch`: the exact body each driver builds, the id each returns, both error shapes, the console fallback, and the production guard refusing it. Three more cover `sandboxAddressFor`. `lint`, `typecheck` and the full unit suite green — 2,722 tests, up from 2,711. The notification, message and comms-threading e2e specs were run to confirm the swap is invisible locally, which is the whole point of the fallback.

**What it left behind.**
- **Neither driver has ever been executed against a real Resend or Twilio account.** That was D-15's stated objection to writing them, and it is still true — the owner's two external workstreams (a verified sending domain with SPF/DKIM, an approved 10DLC brand and campaign) have not been started. What has changed is that shipping them is now safe rather than merely optimistic: an unconfigured production deploy suppresses visibly instead of pretending. **The first real send is still an untested code path, and should be watched.**
- ~~**`NOTIFICATIONS_SANDBOX_TO` is one address for both channels.**~~ **Fixed in the same item, an hour later, because the owner's answer changed the arithmetic.** It was written up as a documented footgun on the reasoning that a comment was cheaper than touching a tested contract — then the owner said they hold both Resend and Twilio credentials and want both drivers exercised, which turns "documented" into *run the whole demo walk twice, once per channel*. The variable now takes one address per channel, comma-separated, and `sandboxAddressFor(channel, addresses)` picks between them on whether the value contains an `@`. **A single value still redirects every channel**, exactly as before, so nothing that was configured yesterday behaves differently today — and a mismatched single value still fails at the provider rather than going on to the real tenant, which is the direction to fail in. Three tests, and `deliverOverChannel` is the only consumer.
- **A synchronous `21610` does not record an opt-out.** If Twilio rejects the API call outright because the recipient has sent STOP, no message exists and no status callback ever arrives — so the carrier opt-out list (R-054) never learns what the send just discovered, and the next attempt fails the same way. It is recorded as a FAILED delivery with code `21610`, so it is visible, and `recordOptOut` has no source value that fits an outbound rejection. Worth a small item.
- **No retry policy.** A `FAILED` delivery stays failed; nothing re-queues it. `failureCode` was built to be branched on and nothing branches on it yet — a rate-limit failure and a bad address are treated identically, and only the second deserves that.

## R-105: walk the demo in a browser
**Commit:** 77bc17126ba1e2e9480c0dd8fa8e7fa5bb446827  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

**The checkpoint Milestone 10 owed.** R-100a, R-100b and R-100c each end with the same sentence — nobody has opened these screens — and D-28's rule is that a walk is what catches what no test is looking for. It caught seven things. Three are in the product.

**How it was walked.** Signed in as a real owner, against a real seeded database, through a real browser: 78 staff routes, the 10 tenant-portal routes and the vendor magic link, recording each page's status, its `h1`, its rendered text and its console errors. No 404s, no 500s, nothing that crashed. Every defect below is a page that returned 200 and was wrong.

**The database is LOCAL, and that is a decision rather than a convenience.** `.env.demo` holds a `rental_demo` on localhost and is loaded BEFORE `.env.local` — dotenv-cli's first-file-wins, the same trick `.env.test` already uses — so it overrides the database and inherits every other variable. Two things it is deliberately not: not the Neon dev branch (which had **zero of 87 migrations applied**, so "the dev database" was a fiction), and not `rental_test`, because a demo seed writing tickets, leases and ledger rows into the suite's own database is the shared-database bug CLAUDE.md warns about twice. `npm run dev:demo` is the one new script.

### What it found

**1. `npm run dev` served this repo on :3000 — the self-storage app's port.** `apps/web/package.json` had a bare `next dev`, and the first attempt at this walk landed on 3001 because the sibling project was already holding 3000. CLAUDE.md says this repo owns 3100 "and that is now the config default", but that was only ever true of `playwright.config.ts`; the bare scripts were never covered. Now `next dev -p ${PORT:-3100}` and the same for `next start`, so `PORT` still overrides and the default can no longer collide. (Separately, and NOT a repo fix because the file is untracked: `.env.local` still carries `AUTH_URL="http://localhost:3000"`, which points every locally minted magic link, payment link and Twilio `StatusCallback` at the storage app.)

**2. Every move-in proration charge ever written has no audit row.** `chargeMoveInProration` records `ledger.adjusted`, which is on `REASON_REQUIRED`, and passed no reason — so `recordAudit` threw, the caller's deliberately non-fatal `.catch` logged it, and the charge went onto the tenant's ledger with nothing recording who put it there or why. **Nothing was ever going to go red**: the audit is swallowed by design, so the only symptom in the entire system was one console line, four rows deep in a seed log, which is where this was found. The reason is now `proration.description` — the same sentence PAY-08 puts on the tenant's own ledger, so the audit and what the tenant was told cannot drift. `proration.test.ts` now asserts the ROW, not the absence of a throw, because the throw was already being swallowed.

**3. An eviction case said "Notice not yet served" while displaying the served notice — and could never be filed.** `attachableNotices` offered `PAY_OR_QUIT` and `NOTICE_TO_VACATE`; `cureClockFor` counted only the first. Two lists reading the same free-form `Notice.type` and disagreeing — R-036b's `VERIFIED` trap exactly, which CLAUDE.md already says is never one edit. `readyToFile` refused the filing for ever with *"Attach the pay-or-quit notice to this case"*, with the notice attached and on screen. **Owner-decided as D-148: both types start the clock**, from `CURE_NOTICE_TYPES` in core, read by the query and by the picker. The reason is the default jurisdiction — Tex. Prop. Code §24.005 names the non-payment instrument a notice to vacate and Texas has no separate pay-or-quit at all, so an operator picking the type their own statute names must not dead-end. The narrower fix (drop the type from the picker, reseed) was smaller and was rejected. It costs nothing where both exist: the clock runs from the earliest good service, so a later notice to vacate cannot move a date an earlier pay-or-quit set.

**4. `/leases/[id]/deposit` rendered its empty state with no `h1` at all** — the heading lived only in the branch below the early return. One page in the whole walk with no heading, which is what a per-route `h1` check is for.

**5. `/tasks` — "My day" — was completely empty.** Zero tasks and a portfolio roll-up of six properties by three columns of zeroes, on the screen a PM opens first and the only work queue this product has (D-9). The seed now **derives** tasks from what the other three stories already built — book the vendor for each `ASSIGNED` work order, verify and close the `WORK_COMPLETE` one (dated two days ago, because a queue with nothing late in it does not show what the overdue column is for), walk the scheduled inspection, decide the renewals the dashboard is already counting. Six tasks, five of them due today or overdue. Derived rather than written down on purpose: a fourth hand-written map would drift from the three above it, and a task naming a work order the maintenance story stopped seeding is a demo bug nobody finds until they are standing in front of somebody.

**6. `/money` reported "Never synced" for all five payers it had just provisioned.** `provisionLeaseBilling` creates the subscription; only the lifecycle sweep writes `lastSyncedAt`, and nothing ran it. The seed now runs the product's own `syncLease` once per billed lease, last, after the replay — so what it reconciles against is the state every event left behind. It reads "In step" because it asked Stripe, not because the seed wrote a breadcrumb.

**7. `/inspections/new` refused to work at all** — "No checklists yet. Build one first." — with two walked inspections sitting on the list behind it, and `/messages/templates` was empty. Both are now seeded, and the checklist is threaded onto the inspections (`Inspection.templateId`) so the detail page names what was walked.

**What that says about the seed, and it is the transferable part.** Three of the four demo gaps were screens the seed had written rows *around* rather than *through*: inspections built from inline item plans and never from the reusable checklist a human would have had to make first. R-100a's lesson was that a status the enum has and a list does not read is invisible; this one is a step earlier — a row the product would have made you create first, that the seed skipped.

**What it decided.**
- **D-148**, above: both notice types start the cure clock, one shared `CURE_NOTICE_TYPES`.
- **The demo walks against a local `rental_demo`, never the Neon dev branch and never `rental_test`.** The seed replays 42 Stripe events and provisions five subscriptions; each of those was a round trip to us-east-2 through a pooler, for the same reason `.env.test` moved local.
- **Tasks are derived from the other stories, never a fourth map.** They are also deleted by `--reset` on BOTH branches, sticky included: a retired property keeps its inspections and its notices because those are the record, but "chase the vendor at a property that no longer exists" is not something to leave on anybody's day.
- **The checklist is retired-and-renamed with `defaultForType` cleared, not deleted, when a property is sticky.** That column is UNIQUE, so a retired checklist still holding `PERIODIC` would refuse the *next* run's template rather than the next run's delete. The message template needs none of that and is deleted outright — nothing in the seed sends from it.

**What it was verified against.** `lint`, `typecheck` and the full unit suite green — 2,723 tests, up from 2,722 (`demo-seed.test.ts` now holds the seeded template against core's closed merge-field catalogue, because an unknown `{{field}}` is refused at SEND time and would fail in front of an audience). `evictions.spec.ts` gained the D-148 case and was run with `deposit-disposition.spec.ts`. The demo was then reset and reseeded from scratch and every fixed screen re-walked: "Cure period running. Runs from 2026-08-22", "In step · 2026-08-25", "5 tasks due today or overdue", a checklist picker with a checklist in it.

**What it left behind.**
- **`.env.local`'s `AUTH_URL` still says 3000.** Untracked and the owner's to change; a link minted locally still points at the storage app.
- **The token-gated public routes were not walked** — `apply/[token]`, `prescreen/[token]`, `sign/[token]`, `showings/[token]`, `pay/[token]`, `vendor/bid/[token]`. The demo seed mints none of those links, which is itself the finding: six stranger-facing screens with no way into them from a seeded demo. Golden Path 4 covers the stranger's path in the suite, so this is a demo gap rather than an untested one.
- **`/claims`, `/abandonment` and `/confidential` are empty by design and were left empty.** A confidential case seeded into a demo is a screen somebody screenshots.
- **In dev, every page logs `eval() is not supported ... Content-Security-Policy`.** React's dev runtime needs `unsafe-eval` and the policy does not grant it. Harmless in production (the e2e suite runs a production build and is silent), but it is noise on every page of a dev-mode walk.
- **A `--reset` leaves the retired checklist on `/inspections/templates`**, the same way retired vendors and PM schedules already linger. Consistent with what was there, and still one more row per reset on a screen an operator reads.

## R-106: a failed delivery is not a finished delivery
**Commit:** 21f8a822ce20d302ac31447793957d39a1f60308  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

R-104's two leftovers, and they are one item because they meet in the same `catch`. **(a)** A `FAILED` delivery stayed failed for ever and nothing re-queued it — `failureCode` was written in four places, rendered in three, and branched on in none, so a Twilio 500 and a disconnected handset were treated identically and both were permanent. **(b)** When Twilio refuses the API call outright because the recipient replied STOP, no message is created, no `MessageSid` exists and no status callback is ever posted — so `/api/sms/status`, which is where the carrier opt-out list (R-054) learns about 21610 today, is never called at all. The send discovered a fact about the recipient and threw it away, and the next send discovered it again.

**What it built.**

**The retry decision is pure and in core, split across the two vocabularies it actually belongs to.** `isPermanentFailure` and `retryDelayMinutes` sit in `packages/core/comms/delivery-status.ts`, beside the `isOptOutErrorCode` that already reads exactly these codes; `NEVER_AUTO_RETRY_CATEGORIES` / `mayAutoRetry` sit in `packages/core/notifications/categories.ts`, beside `LOCKED_CATEGORIES`. They are combined in one branch in `dispatchPendingNotifications`, which is the only place both are known. Neither package imports the other.

**A retryable failure parks on `DEFERRED` with a `sendAfter`, which is the column quiet hours already uses.** Both answer the same question — the earliest instant the drain may send this — and the drain already picks up a `DEFERRED` row whose time has passed, so the hourly cron became the retry engine without a new table, a new job or a new status. **`failedAt` and `failureCode` are written even when we are going to retry**, so the row says both things a reader needs: waiting until T, and the last refusal was this at that time. Clearing them would make a message that has been failing for four hours indistinguishable from one merely held until morning.

**The opt-out branch is in `deliver.ts`'s single `catch`, not in the Twilio driver.** That is the one place every channel's failure passes through, so `sendThreadMessage()` gets it as well as `notify()` — a driver-local fix would have been correct for one adapter and left the next one to rediscover the hole, which is the same "shared, not per-path" argument D-9 made for the one `Task` queue and R-054 made for this exact list. It records against the address the provider **actually refused**, not the intended one: in a sandbox environment those differ, and opting out a tenant because a developer's test handset said STOP would block a real person.

**What it decided.**

- **No third `SmsOptOutSource` value; `CARRIER_CALLBACK` covers a synchronous rejection, and the schema comment now says so out loud.** The backlog asked for this call explicitly. The fact this column records is *which side learned of the opt-out, us or them*, and both a status callback and an API refusal are them. A third value would split one fact across two rows, cost a migration, and require finding every list that reads the enum — CLAUDE.md's "adding a value to a status enum is never one edit" cutting against the change rather than for it. `reason` already carries `twilio:<code>` for anyone who needs to tell them apart.
- **The retryable set is a default-on with a named exception list, not the reverse.** Anything not in `PERMANENT_FAILURE_CODES` is retried, because the defect being closed is that a rate limit was treated like a dead address, and of the two the rate limit is the common one. The permanent list holds the codes where retrying is not merely useless but *wrong*: opt-outs, unusable numbers, Resend's validation names, and — **the dangerous one** — `no_sid`/`no_id`, which mean the provider **accepted** the message and returned something we could not read an id out of. A retry there sends it twice.
- **`NEVER_AUTO_RETRY_CATEGORIES` is `legal_notice` and `entry_notice`, and is deliberately NOT `LOCKED_CATEGORIES`.** Locked means "you may not switch this off"; this means "we may not repeat it without you". They share two members and disagree about the other two: `maintenance_emergency` is locked *because* it must reach somebody, so a failed gas-leak page is the one that most wants retrying, and `lease_signature` is a link to a page. Serving a notice is a legally operative act — it starts a clock somebody is counting days against, and a second copy carries a second timestamp, so which service is the operative one becomes a question a court asks and this system cannot answer.
- **What happens to those instead is D-38's task, one step later.** A notice we could not text at all already raises `serve_notice_offline`; a notice the provider refused is the same obligation unmet, discovered at send time rather than decide time. Both land on the **same** task: `createTask` is idempotent on (type, subjectId, businessDate) and the subject id is the notification's own idempotency key with the channel suffix stripped, so a failed SMS and a failed email about one notice are one piece of work for one person. `raiseBlockedNoticeTask` became `raiseNoticeTask` with the title as a parameter (and lost a `recipient` argument that was never read).
- **A retry is pushed past quiet hours.** NOTIF-05 does not stop applying because the first attempt failed — without this, a send that fails at 20:55 local comes back four hours later as a text at one in the morning. It costs one property lookup on a path only failures reach, and `bypassesQuietHours` still exempts the emergency page.
- **Three attempts, at 15 / 60 / 240 minutes, then stop.** Coarse on purpose: the drain is an hourly cron (D-3), so anything finer is rounded up to the next tick and a precise exponential curve would describe a resolution the system does not have. A provider still refusing after five hours is not a blip and wants a human.

**What it was verified against.** `lint` (0 errors), `typecheck`, `npm run db:drift` ("No difference detected" — the schema changes are `///` comments only, so no migration), and the full unit suite green at **2,740 tests**, up from 2,736: eight new assertions across `delivery-status.test.ts` (the permanent/retryable split and the backoff schedule), `notifications.test.ts` (`mayAutoRetry` is not the locked list; a transient failure parks on `DEFERRED` keeping its `failureCode`; `no_id` never retries; the budget runs out; a retry does not land in quiet hours) and `opt-out.test.ts` (a synchronous 21610 records the opt-out, a 30003 does not, and a refused entry notice is never retried but does raise the task). `notifications.spec.ts`, `announcements.spec.ts`, `comms-threading.spec.ts` and `messages.spec.ts` were run together: **58 passed, 58 listed**, exit 0.

**What it left behind.**
- **`MessageDelivery` — a staff member's own reply in a thread — still has no retry at all.** It gets the opt-out recording for free by sharing `deliver.ts`, which is the half that had to be shared, but there is no sweep over that table and a failed reply stays `FAILED`. That is a bigger question than a backoff: a human is standing there and the honest answer may be telling them it failed rather than retrying behind their back.
- **Nothing surfaces a delivery that exhausted its retries.** It is `FAILED` in the log, and for a legal notice a task now exists — but for a rent reminder that failed four times, the only reader is somebody who goes looking. The `remaining` counter R-102 added is the instrument that would say whether that matters.
- **The backoff is not jittered.** A provider outage fails every queued message at the same tick and retries all of them at the same instant fifteen minutes later. Harmless at this portfolio size and a real thundering herd at a much larger one.

## R-037b: a surcharge you cannot prove is lawful
**Commit:** 3c53e40  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

R-037 shipped the card pass-through behind `JurisdictionRule.cardSurchargePermitted`, a boolean. Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §604A.003 permits a surcharge on a **credit** card and bars one on a **debit or stored-value** card. A boolean cannot say that, so the Texas row said `true` — and every debit card paying rent through this product was surcharged unlawfully. The gap was not undiscovered: R-037's own PROGRESS entry names it, and the seeded rule's `notes` field has apologised for it since. It was recorded, and it was still charging money.

**What it built.**

**`CardSurchargePolicy` is `NONE` / `CREDIT_ONLY` / `ALL`, and `cardFeeFor` takes the card's funding type.** `surchargePermittedFor(policy, funding)` in `packages/core/payments/fees.ts` is the whole decision: `NONE` never, `ALL` always, `CREDIT_ONLY` only when funding is `credit`. **`prepaid` is barred alongside `debit`** — §604A.003 names "debit or stored value card", and a check that only tested `'debit'` would have let stored value through silently.

**`unknown` is the ordinary funding value, not an error path, and it forgoes the fee.** Stripe reports funding only once a payment method exists; PAY-01 requires the number be disclosed **before** the tenant picks a rail. So the quote genuinely cannot know, both call sites pass `unknown`, and **Texas therefore charges no card surcharge at all.** That is the deliberate outcome, not a regression: charging and hoping the card was credit is a violation on every debit card that comes through, and this product has no way to tell afterwards which those were.

**`funding` has no default parameter.** A default of `unknown` would let a future caller that *does* know silently forget to pass it; a default of `credit` would quietly reintroduce the defect. Three call sites; each is made to say what it actually knows.

**The audit row on a payment intent now carries `cardSurchargePolicy` and `cardFunding`.** A zero fee under `CREDIT_ONLY` is the correct outcome, so a trail recording only the amount could not distinguish "we could not prove your card was credit" from "this state forbids the fee" — different defences, six months later, from the same silence.

**What it decided** (D-149).

- **The three-state route, not the surcharge-provider one.** The backlog offered integrating Yeeld or InterPayments. Both are third-party, US-only and in preview, for a fee this portfolio can simply forgo — and D-12 says core computes any number a statute could change, which a vendor computing it would invert.
- **And not "quote the fee after the payment method is attached" either.** That was the backlog's own second option and it trades a compliance risk for a worse disclosure; PAY-01 wants the number before the choice. The quote and the charge pass the **same** `unknown`, so the number shown is the number taken.
- **The migration backfills every `true` to `CREDIT_ONLY`, not to `ALL`** — which is not the behaviour-preserving choice, deliberately. `true` meant "permitted, debit-vs-credit not distinguished"; it was never a reviewed statement that debit surcharging is lawful, so preserving it as `ALL` would launder an unreviewed assumption into a name that now asserts something specific. `CREDIT_ONLY` is safe under both readings: in a state that permits everything we forgo revenue, and in a state that bars debit we obey it. Under-collecting is a cost; over-collecting here is unlawful, and only one of those two errors is ours to choose.
- **The schema default is `NONE`, where the boolean's was `true`.** A rule row created without an answer must not be read as permission.

**The bug this item would otherwise have detonated.** `railsFor` took a `cardPermitted` flag, and its only caller fed it `cardSurchargePermitted` — so **a jurisdiction that forbade the surcharge had card payments closed altogether**, with the tenant told "Card payments are not available for this property." Those are different facts: a surcharge ban means the *owner* absorbs the cost, which `cardFeeFor` had always returned correctly and the caller then threw away. Setting Texas to `CREDIT_ONLY` would have turned card payments off across the portfolio. Nothing in the schema says a property does not take cards, so the flag had no honest source and is **gone rather than rewired**; if an owner preference for that ever exists it arrives as a column and the signature changes then.

**What it was verified against.** `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, `npm run build`, and `npm run db:drift` ("No difference detected"). Unit suite green at **2,745 tests**, up from 2,740 — five new: the CREDIT_ONLY refusal across all four funding values, that `ALL` still surcharges debit (the assertion that fails if somebody simplifies the policy back to a boolean), that `NONE` never surcharges whatever the card turns out to be, that the decision reports the funding it decided against including on the zero-amount short circuit, and that `railsFor` keeps the card rail open. `pay.spec.ts` run in full: **30 listed, 30 passed**, exit 0, up from 28 — the existing disclosure and intent-trail tests moved to a jurisdiction seeded `ALL` (in state `XS`, a code no other file uses), and two new tests assert the Texas truth: no fee line with the card rail still enabled, and an audit row that records *why* the fee was zero. The migration was applied to both `rental_test` and `rental_demo`.

**What it left behind.**
- **Texas collects no card surcharge until something knows the funding type before quoting.** That is a revenue decision the correct legal answer forced, not an oversight. Getting it back means restructuring the pay flow to create the payment method first, read `card.funding`, then size the intent — a change to the flow, not to the rule, and a real item whenever the money matters more than the disclosure ordering PAY-01 asks for.
- **A saved payment method's funding type is knowable today and is not stored.** `LeasePayer.defaultPaymentMethodId` exists, and Stripe would report funding at attach time. Nothing was built for it because **no saved-card path surcharges** — `cardFeeFor` is reached only from the two portal call sites, never from the autopay invoice path — so capturing it would be building the vehicle for a fee nobody currently charges.
- **`reviewedBy` on the Texas rule is still null.** The backlog row says this item needs the attorney review D-4 requires and not just an engineering call; the engineering half is what shipped. The rule now states the statute correctly rather than approximately, which is a better thing to hand a lawyer, but it is still unreviewed configuration.
- **There is still no admin UI for the surcharge fields.** `rule-form.tsx` does not render them, so `cardSurchargePolicy` and `cardSurchargeMaxBps` are seed-only — which is why this migration needed no form change, and is a gap whenever a second state arrives.

## R-107a: focus you can see, and focus that survives a submit
**Commit:** 564107c  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

The first spend of the 2026-08-25 accessibility audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-25-accessibility-ux.md`, 75 findings across all 88 routes). This is the shared-layer half: three defects that each live in one place and reach every screen. The 37-caller live-region sweep is R-107b.

**What it built.**

**A focus ring that names its own colour, everywhere.** Tailwind v4 defaults `--tw-ring-color` to `currentcolor` and `--tw-ring-offset-color` to white. On a `text-background` button `currentColor` **is** the background — so thirteen buttons drew a white ring behind a white gap on a white page, at **1.00:1**, having already removed the browser's own indicator with `focus-visible:outline-none`. Not "low contrast": invisible. It survived thirteen copies because the class list reads as though it is handled.

**Ten further call sites were relying on `currentcolor` happening to be dark** — passing by luck, one restyle away from breaking silently. They were fixed too, and that is what made the rule checkable: *every* `focus-visible:ring-2` now names its colour.

**`SubmitButton` is `aria-disabled`, never `disabled`.** A focused element that becomes `disabled` is blurred by the browser, so ~108 forms threw keyboard focus to `<body>` on every press — and `disabled` also removes it from the accessibility tree, so the swap to "Working…" was announced to nobody and `FormAlerts` then announced the result into a region the user was no longer near. `aria-busy` conveys the state; a click guard does the one thing `disabled` was actually needed for. `opacity-60` went with it: faded primary over white is about **2.2:1**, so the pending label was least readable exactly when it was the only thing worth reading.

**Tokens re-toned, and `--border` split from `--input` for the first time.** `--input` 0.922 → 0.72 (1.26:1 → 3.05:1) and `--ring` 0.708 → 0.55 (2.59:1 → 4.63:1) against white; the dark `--input` alpha 18% → 40%, which composited to 1.64:1 and is the easier one to miss because an alpha looks unremarkable beside a solid colour. `--border` deliberately stays soft — 1.4.11 draws exactly that distinction and a divider is decoration. The base `* { outline-ring/50 }` loses its alpha: at 50% over white it computed to **1.54:1**, and it was the only focus indicator on any control setting none of its own — `CheckboxField` was one until now.

**What it decided** (D-150).

- **A source-walking test, not an e2e one.** `apps/web/components/focus-visibility.test.ts` enforces all three rules. Focus visibility is a computed style at a moment a test cannot easily hold, and the real failure mode is a fourteenth copy in a future diff — a source property, caught the same way and for the same reason `app/route-guards.test.ts` catches a missing route guard. It found my own comment text on its first run, and I verified it fails on an injected multi-line violation before trusting it.
- **`PRIMARY_BUTTON_CLASSES` lives in a plain module**, not in `auth-form.tsx`: half the call sites are server components, and every export of a `'use client'` module becomes a client reference rather than the value. `npm run build` is what confirms that, which is why it is in the gate.
- **Layout classes stayed at the call sites.** They differ (`self-start` / `w-fit` / `flex-1`) and are none of the shared definition's business.

**Two real suite bugs found while verifying, and they are the reason this took three sweeps.**

- **`renewals.spec.ts` was failing on every sweep and reporting as flaky. Fixed here.** The file has two tests; both seed a rent-increase cap for the same state code `ZZ`, and they seed *different* ones (10% and 5%) because one asserts an increase inside the cap and the other over it. `@@unique([state, jurisdiction, version])` means only one row can exist and `rulesFor` reads every rule for a state before choosing, so whichever landed second decided the answer for both — the within-cap test submitted 6.7% against the other's 5% cap, was correctly refused, never redirected, and sat on `waitForURL` for the full 60s. **`retries: 1` is what hid it**: fail-then-pass reports as flaky and a run with flaky tests still exits 0. Confirmed three ways before touching it — reproduces with `--retries=0` in both projects, passes when run alone, and reproduces identically with all of R-107a stashed. Each test now owns its state code.
- **`workorders.spec.ts`'s axe test had no headroom.** Three full scans in one test, the third on the heaviest page in the product; **measured at 42.3s and 42.5s idle against the 60s default**. It exceeded the budget under five workers on both attempts and reported as a `page.evaluate` error that reads like an axe problem rather than a budget one. Now `test.setTimeout(180_000)` with the measurement written beside it — the fourth time this shape has been diagnosed in this repo.

**What it was verified against.** `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, `npm run build`, unit suite green at **2,748 tests** (2,744 passed, 4 skipped), up from 2,745 — three new, one per invariant. Full e2e sweep: **1,034 listed, 1,026 passed + 8 skipped, 0 failed, 0 flaky, exit 0.** The two earlier sweeps that were not clean are described above; both causes were pre-existing and neither was an accessibility violation.

**What it left behind.**
- **R-107b is the other half** and is the largest single count in the audit: 37 hand-rolled `{state.error && <p role="alert">}` blocks that announce nothing, including a declined card and a failed application fee. **Its verification item comes first** (audit angle ⑳): every live region in this product relies on `display: contents` not removing the element from the accessibility tree — historically browsers did, iOS Safari + VoiceOver is the portal's primary target, and nobody here has ever checked. If that assumption is wrong the sweep is 37 no-ops on top of R-101's, and no automated test could tell you.
- **Nine components hand-roll their own `disabled={pending}` button** and still blur focus on submit, keeping `disabled:opacity-60` with it. They share the defect `SubmitButton` just shed but not its code; rewiring each one's pending logic is its own change.
- **`--border` stays at 1.26:1** as a decorative hairline. Permitted by 1.4.11, and a judgement a designer may want to revisit rather than one a test should freeze.
- **R-108 records an undiagnosed flake in `abandonment.spec.ts`** — a 26-value random state code on a unique key, reproducing 1 in 24 with retries off. What is proven and what is not are written down separately, because the symptom is a timeout rather than the constraint violation a collision should produce, and that gap has to be explained before anything is changed.

## R-108: the constraint that was never going to fire
**Commit:** 46e4268  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

The row was filed undiagnosed on purpose — *"a fix aimed at a guessed cause is the thing this repo's own notes warn against"* — with what was proven and what was not written down separately. The diagnosis is that **the row's own premise was wrong**, and so was R-107a's when it fixed the same shape in `renewals.spec.ts`.

**What it decided, because everything else follows from it.**

`@@unique([state, jurisdiction, version])` does not refuse a repeated state code, and never did. Every fixture rule is statewide, so `jurisdiction` is NULL, and **Postgres treats NULLs as DISTINCT** in a unique index. Proven with SQL rather than reasoned about: two `('QQ', NULL, 1)` rows insert into `rental_test` inside one transaction, `INSERT 0 2`, no error.

So a repeat draw does not collide — it creates a **second** statewide rule. `rulesFor` fetches every rule for the state and `selectApplicableRule` breaks the `effectiveFrom` tie with `if (!best || rule.effectiveFrom > best.effectiveFrom)`, which keeps whichever row `findMany` returned first. There is no `orderBy`, so which test's statute governs is a race. Nothing throws anywhere.

**That closes the gap the row demanded be explained.** A collision does not produce a constraint violation; it produces a page rendering the *other* branch, correctly, from another test's numbers:

- `belongingsStorageDays: null` inherited as `30` → the case is disposable, so `period_unknown`'s "is not configured in this system" never appears → **15s** `expect` timeout.
- `30` inherited as `null` → `period_unknown` → the disposal form never renders → `fill('What was done with it')` waits out the whole **60s test timeout**. That is the exact symptom the row recorded.
- The fourth test reads no storage period at all, which is why it never failed and why "a different test each time" was as far as anyone got.

**Proven by making it fail** (the R-099 standard). `stateCode()` pinned to a constant, full spec, `--retries=0`: **3 failed, 5 passed, zero unique-constraint errors** — two of the failures at 1.0m on `disposal is allowed once the period has run`, one at 17.1s on `THE OTHER GATE`. Both gates passed in the other browser project in the same run, which is the race showing itself.

**What it built.** `uniqueStateCode()` in `e2e/fixtures.ts`, beside `uniquePhone()` and for the same reason. Genuinely unique rather than sequential — deliberately the opposite of `uniquePhone`'s own rule, and the comment says why: a phone number has a format to fit inside, a state code has no length constraint anywhere in the repo, so there is nothing to gain by gambling at all. It is unique across workers, across browser projects and against rows a crashed run left behind. `abandonment.spec.ts` also picked up `uniqueClientHeaders()`, which it had hand-rolled.

**Verified:** `lint` (0 errors, same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, unit suite **2,744 passed + 4 skipped of 2,748, exit 0**, and `abandonment.spec.ts` at `--repeat-each=3 --retries=0` — **24 listed, 24 passed, 0 flaky**, the same multiplier that surfaced the flake in the first place.

**Two unit failures found on the way, both the shared database and neither this change** (nothing here is loaded by vitest). Filed as **R-109**; diagnosed rather than guessed at, because that is what this item was about.

- **`reissue.test.ts` counts `authToken` rows globally.** `prisma.authToken.count({ where: { purpose: 'VENDOR_WORK_ORDER' } })` before and after, asserting nothing new was minted — red the moment any other file mints a vendor token between the two reads, which is what happened (1842 against an expected 1841). It passes alone every time. This is the exact rule CLAUDE.md already carries from `inbound-email.test.ts`.
- **`notifications.test.ts`'s global-sweep test fails after any recent suite run.** R-102 gave it a `beforeAll` retiring QUEUED rows **older than an hour**, and an hour is longer than it takes one suite run to leave 4,044 fresh ones. Measured: 4,044 QUEUED deliveries, **every one under an hour old**, so the retirement matched nothing and the sweep could not reach its own rows. Draining them by hand and re-running the file alone: 21 passed. Then the full suite, green. So the fix R-102 shipped works only on the first run in any hour, which is not a condition anybody can be expected to keep.

**What it left behind.**
- **`notice-to-vacate.spec.ts` (`YY`), `pay.spec.ts` (`XS`), `renewals.spec.ts` (`ZU`/`ZO`) still use fixed codes and still create duplicate rows** — one per test per browser project. They are safe today only because each file always seeds the *same* rule body under a given code, so the arbitrary tie-break picks between identical rows. One edit that varies a number under an existing code re-creates this bug exactly, which is what happened to `renewals.spec.ts`. Not swept here: they are green, and widening a diagnosis item into four working specs is how a fix breaks something it was not asked to touch. The guard is the helper plus the CLAUDE.md rule.
- **The database still permits two statewide rules in force on the same day**, and `selectApplicableRule` still resolves that silently. `createRuleVersion` cannot produce it (version arithmetic, and a new `effectiveFrom` must be later than the one it supersedes), so this is a test-fixture hazard rather than a live one. Closing it at the database — `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, Postgres 15+ — would break the three specs above on their next run and would report schema drift, since Prisma cannot express it. That is a real item, not a footnote to this one.
- **`docs/PROGRESS.md`'s R-107a entry describes the `renewals.spec.ts` mechanism as "only one row can exist"**, which is the same wrong belief. Its fix — a state code per test — was right for the wrong reason. Left as written; this entry is the correction.

## R-109: two tests that only passed on a quiet database
**Commit:** 1ba0ff3  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

Both were diagnosed in R-108 and deliberately left unfixed there. Neither is a product bug; both are the same class of defect — a test whose correctness depends on what else happens to be in the shared database — and one of them was a *fix* for that class that did not work.

**What it built.**

**(a) `reissue.test.ts` counts its own tokens.** `prisma.authToken.count({ where: { purpose: 'VENDOR_WORK_ORDER' } })` before and after, asserting nothing was minted, is red the moment any other file mints a vendor token between the two reads — 1842 against an expected 1841, and green alone every time. `seedJob` now records the work orders it creates and the count is scoped to them. This is not quite the usual substitution, because the assertion is about the ABSENCE of a row rather than the presence of one, and the comment says why the scope is still sound: the only mint path in `reissueOnExpiry` is `issueVendorLink(workOrder.id, …)` for a work order resolved from the token.

**(b) `notifications.test.ts` retires debris by OWNERSHIP, not by age.** R-102 gave the one deliberately-global sweep a `beforeAll` that suppressed QUEUED deliveries older than an hour. The argument was sound — nothing a concurrently-running spec is asserting on can be an hour old — and the result was useless: one suite run leaves thousands of rows and finishes in minutes, so inside the hour the predicate matched **nothing** and the sweep paid for the whole backlog anyway.

**What it decided.** The hour was standing in for *"nobody is still using this row"*, and the database already records that directly. Every spec here **deactivates** its property in `afterAll` — it cannot delete it, because `Notification` is append-only and the FK is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, which is an UPDATE the trigger refuses — so an inactive property is a spec that has finished and an active one is a spec that may still be running. The predicate is now `notification: { property: { active: false } }`. That is a **stronger** guarantee than the hour gave, not a weaker one: it cannot touch a live fixture at any age, and it fires on debris the moment the debris exists. Lowering the number was the wrong move and is the reason the row said this was a decision.

Checked before relying on it: **all 235,013 notifications written to `rental_test` in the last two days hang off an inactive property, and none off an active one**; only 133 of 19,150 properties are still active, all of them wreckage from crashed runs. The three files that deactivate a property inside a test rather than in `afterAll` (`rubs.test.ts` ×2, `punch-list.test.ts`'s `afterEach`) all do it *after* that test's assertions, so none of them can retire a row it is about to read.

A notification with no property at all — a portfolio-wide digest — has no ownership signal and is deliberately left alone.

**Proven by making it fire** (the R-099 standard), against 3,109 rows of real debris left by the preceding full run:

| | QUEUED | SENT | SUPPRESSED | file duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before the run | 3,109 | 167,929 | 144,430 | — |
| after the run | **0** | **167,929 — unchanged** | 147,539 (+3,109, reason `stale_test_fixture`) | **1.47s** |

Nothing was sent. The immediately preceding run under the old predicate did the opposite: it sent its 1,302-row backlog (SENT 165,061 → 166,363) and spent 4.40s doing it, with the global-sweep test alone taking 2.59s.

**Verified:** `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, and the full unit suite — **2,744 passed + 4 skipped of 2,748 across 204 files + 1 skipped, exit 0**, reconciling against R-108's baseline. No e2e spec was touched, so the 596 are left to CI per CLAUDE.md.

**What it left behind.**
- **The drain runs in one file's `beforeAll`, so it only clears what existed when `notifications.test.ts` started.** Rows left by files that finish later in the same run survive to the next run. That is hygiene, not correctness — the sweep test's cost is now bounded by one run's output rather than by the age of the database, which is what R-102 wanted.
- **`e2e/cron.spec.ts` is the second global sweep and has no drain of its own.** It hits `/api/cron` over HTTP, which sweeps unfiltered, so it pays for whatever the e2e run itself has queued. It is affordable today because `npm test` runs first in the gate and now genuinely empties the table; if the e2e sweep ever times out, this is where to look and the same ownership predicate is the fix.
- **A notification with a null `propertyId` can never be retired.** None exist in this database today. If portfolio-wide digests start queueing in tests, they will accumulate.
- **Three `afterAll` hooks timed out at 10s in the first full run of this session** (`sms-intake`, `triage-consumer`, `job-consumer`) — all three `deleteMany` calls with nested relation filters, all three green alone and green in the clean re-run. The cause was mine and not the code's: `lint` and `typecheck` were running against the same laptop at the same time, which is the load the conventions warn about. Recorded because the symptom — three unrelated files failing in teardown with zero test failures — reads like a code defect and is not one.

## R-107b: the live regions that announce nothing
**Commit:** 785270f  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

Audit item 4, the largest single count in `docs/audits/2026-08-25-accessibility-ux.md`. `{state.error && <p role="alert">…}` inserts the region and its text as one new node, and a live region announces CHANGES TO ITSELF — so a node that arrives already-populated is not a change and assistive technology routinely says nothing. R-101 fixed this in `FormAlerts` and R-031 fixed it in `FieldError`; these were the callers that hand-rolled the broken shape instead of importing the fix.

**What it built.** **34 regions across 28 files** now use `FieldError` (field-level messages) or `LiveRegion` (form-level errors, confirmations), both of which mount unconditionally. No new component: the sweep is a net **-49 lines** of JSX. It reaches every surface the audit named — a declined card in `autopay-panel.tsx`, a failed application fee in `fee-payment.tsx`, the portal reply form, the emergency-details form, the photo uploader, the vendor's "show code" refusal, the jurisdiction rule form, the renewal cap, the billing-run sync error and the record-invoice split error.

Two conversions were more than a substitution, because the message was a `return` that replaced the thing it was reporting on:

- **`fee-payment.tsx`** returned early with `<p role="status">Payment submitted…</p>`, so the applicant who had just paid got a new node and silence. Both regions are now mounted for the whole flow and the form hides under them.
- **`listing-inquiry-form.tsx`** did the same with its confirmation. Same fix.

**What it decided.**

**(a) The five `?param` banners are a different problem and were left alone.** `/login?reset=1`, `/account?mfa=required`, `/jurisdiction?versioned=`, `/properties?entityCreated=` and `/portal/maintenance/[id]?emergency=1` all arrive by redirect **from a different route**, so there is no earlier region for the text to change — the whole subtree is new whatever shape it has. Announcing a page you just navigated to is Next's route announcer's job, which is the argument `hold-banner.tsx` already makes in its own comment. `/apply/[token]`'s completion notice is the one that *is* reachable: submitting revalidates the same route, so it was converted.

**(b) The verification item (audit item 12 / angle ⑳) is still open, and the sweep did not wait for it.** Whether `display: contents` keeps an element in the accessibility tree cannot be settled here: there is no screen reader in this environment and both Playwright projects are Chromium. It was not a reason to hold the sweep, because a conditionally-mounted region is broken in **every** engine while `contents` is fixed in all current ones — and after this item, if the assumption ever does prove wrong, it is a two-line change in three primitives instead of an edit in 37 files. Still owed: one VoiceOver-on-iOS pass. Left in the audit as written.

**The real bug found on the way: a `key` on a `<form>` throws its live regions away.** `PropertyForm` bumps `formVersion` and uses it as the form's `key`, deliberately, to repopulate uncontrolled inputs React resets on every action dispatch (R-008's fix, with a long comment). That remount also destroys `FormAlerts` and the duplicate-address warning **on every response**, so R-101's always-mounted regions were new nodes here every single time — the fix was silently undone on this form and nowhere else (`formVersion` appears in exactly one file). The regions are now hoisted out of the keyed `<form>` into a stable wrapper, and the "Save anyway" button reaches the form it submits through the native `form=` attribute rather than by living inside it. The id comes from `useId()`, not a constant, so two of these on one page cannot collide.

**Proven, not assumed.** `properties.spec.ts` now tags the empty region before pressing Create and asserts the warning turned up **in that same DOM node**. Asserting `getByRole('alert')` alone passes just as happily against a freshly-minted region, which is exactly how this defect survived R-101 — the node-identity check is the part of the claim that our code controls and that a test can see. It walks the form's *parent* because every `FieldError` inside the form is also a `role="alert"`, and it avoids a bare `getByRole` because Next injects its own route announcer with that role (`auth.spec.ts` says the same).

**Also fixed, because the same edit is where it lives:** audit item 6's two document uploaders. Both set `aria-invalid` with no `aria-describedby` and an error `<p>` carrying no id, so the field announced "invalid" and the reason was orphaned prose. `FieldError` takes the id; the `aria-describedby` is one attribute on the adjacent line. The other four sites in item 6 were not touched.

**Verified:** `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, the full unit suite — **2,744 passed + 4 skipped of 2,748 across 204 files + 1 skipped**, reconciling exactly against R-109's baseline — and a targeted e2e run over the specs covering every swept component: **341 passed, 1 failed, 2 flaky in 2.9m**. All three of those are one cause and none of them is this item's, which is R-110 below. The full 596 are CI's, per CLAUDE.md.

**Three e2e failures found, one cause, filed as R-110.** `preventive-maintenance.spec.ts`'s batch test signs in as a portfolio-scoped owner and presses Run batch on a brand-new template, which is due for **every unit in that scope** — the spec's own comment says so, and the shared test database currently holds **14,985 units**. So: its own assertion timed out at 15s twice in mobile-chrome (16.2s, 16.5s) and then passed in 2.0s in desktop-chrome, because the first project's batch had already taken what was due; and `workorders.spec.ts` and `vendor-invoice-splits.spec.ts` both died in `afterAll` on `WorkOrder_unitId_fkey`, unable to delete units that another spec's batch had hung work orders off. Alone, the file is 4 passed in 21.2s, both projects — the shared-database signature this repo has now been bitten by four times. The fix is scope, not a longer timeout; raising the 15s buys time that the next thousand units take back (R-102's lesson).

**What it left behind.**
- **R-110** — the batch-scope defect above. Filed, not fixed here: it is a test-suite bug in a spec this item never touched, and widening a sweep into it is how a fix breaks something it was not asked to change.
- **The five cross-route banners above.** They are not fixable by this mechanism; if they are ever worth announcing, the answer is the route announcer or a focus move, not a live region.
- **Audit item 12 / angle ⑳ is unchanged.** Nobody has heard any of this work, R-101's included.
- **Four of audit item 6's six sites** (`translations-panel.tsx`, `delete-form.tsx`, `timeline-section.tsx` ×2) still mark a field invalid without describing why. Not in this item's diff and not worth widening it for.
- **`billing-runs.tsx` reads slightly differently now**: the sync error is its own region and the two non-error states render only when there is no error, rather than as branches of one ternary. That is what it takes for the error to be a change inside a region that was already there.

## R-110: one spec's batch, every other spec's units
**Commit:** f8842a1  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

Filed by R-107b, which found it as three e2e failures in one 341-test run and correctly refused to widen its own sweep into it. Not a product bug: `runPreventiveBatch` doing what MAINT-08 asks — "one action creates the batch across properties" — is the feature. The bug is a spec that asked for it portfolio-wide against a database it shares with 40 other files.

**What it built.** Both tests in `preventive-maintenance.spec.ts` now narrow the property switcher to their own property before pressing **Run batch**, through the same `scopeTo` helper `leasing-analytics.spec.ts` already carries for the same reason (a shared database letting other specs' rows into a portfolio-wide number). Three lines of helper, one call per test.

The assertion got *stronger* rather than looser. It was `/Created \d+ work orders?/` with a comment explaining that an exact count was impossible; it is now `Created 1 work order`, because a brand-new template is due for every unit in scope and the scope is now exactly one unit — so **the count IS the scope**, and asserting it is what fails if this ever regresses to portfolio-wide.

**What it decided.**

**A narrower assignment cannot be the fix, and this is worth writing down because it is the obvious first idea.** The row proposed "a property-scoped operator" as one of two options. It does not work: `runPreventiveBatch` guards on `requirePermission('workorder.write')` with **no resource** — the deliberate coarse-permission-then-scope shape its own header comment describes — and `assignmentCovers` denies a scoped assignment outright when there is no `resource.propertyId` to match. A property- or entity-scoped owner gets redirected to `/no-access` before reaching the batch at all. Making that assignment work would mean changing the guard, which is a product change wearing a test fix's clothes. The switcher is the lever the product actually gives a PM, it is a filter intersected server-side with R-004 on every request, and it required no source change.

**The timing symptom disappeared with the scope, exactly as the row predicted.** 16.2s/16.5s against a 15s deadline in mobile-chrome and 2.0s in desktop-chrome (the second project finding nothing left to do) became **1.6s in both projects, concurrently**. The 15s was never touched — raising it would have bought time the next thousand units take straight back (R-102's lesson).

**Verified:** `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, and the three specs the defect actually involved run together in one sweep — `preventive-maintenance.spec.ts`, `workorders.spec.ts` and `vendor-invoice-splits.spec.ts`: **36 passed in 1.6m**, reconciling exactly against `playwright test --list` (Total: 36 tests in 3 files). Both neighbours' `afterAll` teardowns survived, which is the half of this defect a green preventive-maintenance run on its own would not have proven.

**What it left behind.**
- **The debris already in the shared database is still there.** Every past run of this spec left work orders hanging off other specs' units, and the spec's own `afterAll` only deletes within its own properties. Those rows block deletion of units that are themselves abandoned debris, so nothing live is affected and no cleanup was written — a migration or script that deletes work orders in a test database is a bigger risk than the rows are.
- **No other spec was audited for the same shape.** This one was found by a failing run, not a sweep. A batch or bulk action pressed by a portfolio-scoped actor is the pattern to grep for if it happens again; `scopeTo` is now in two files and is the answer both times.

## R-111: a theme nobody wired up, and a scanner told not to look
**Commit:** 155fc03  ·  **Date:** 2026-08-25

Audit angles ②, ㉑ and ㉒ — the shared-layer remainder after R-107a and R-107b. **This item was built in a previous session that never committed it or wrote this entry;** it was found uncommitted in the working tree at the start of R-112 and is recorded here from its own diff, verified rather than taken on trust.

**What it built.**

**(a) 243 `dark:` utilities across 76 files, deleted.** `@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *))` and a full `.dark` palette existed in `globals.css`, and nothing in the product ever set the class or read `prefers-color-scheme`. Counted from the diff: 243 utilities, 76 files. `globals.css` now opens with a comment saying the product is light-only and what it would take to change that — the palette and the toggle first, `dark:` classes after.

**(b) One `axeScan()` replacing 60 hand-written `AxeBuilder` chains across 40 spec files.** Every one of the 60 wrote `.withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa'])` by hand, and that set **excludes axe's `best-practice` rules** — among them `landmark-no-duplicate-main`. `/portal/pay/history` rendered a `<main>` inside the portal layout's `<main>`: two main landmarks and a skip link resolving to the wrong one, green on every scan. The helper turns `best-practice` on; the nested `<main>` is a `<div>`.

**(c) The admin section nav was an `<aside>`,** which maps to `role="complementary"` — a landmark-navigating screen-reader user hears "complementary" and moves past the only way around the app. One element changed to a `<div>`; the `<nav aria-label="Sections">` inside was already carrying the semantics.

**What it decided.**

**Light-only is now a stated position, not an accident.** A theme nobody wired up is worse than no theme: it makes every reviewer confident about a surface that does not exist. R-107a had *measured and fixed* a 1.64:1 contrast bug in the dark `--input` — real work, on CSS no eye has ever seen.

**The tag filter is itself a defect surface,** which is why the fix is one helper rather than 60 corrected call sites. "axe passes" is a statement about a configuration, not about a page, and 60 identical hand-written configurations is what copying a neighbour produces. A rule that ever has to be off goes in `disableRules` with its reason, never by narrowing the tags back.

**Verified.** The nested `<main>` was proven by restoring it and watching three rules go red — `landmark-main-is-top-level`, `landmark-no-duplicate-main` and `landmark-unique`, the third one the audit had not named. That run happened in the session that built this, which also recorded `lint` (0 errors, the same 14 pre-existing warnings), `typecheck`, the full unit suite at **2,744 passed + 4 skipped of 2,748**, and a 50-test probe green with `best-practice` on. Independently here: the same lint, typecheck and unit numbers, plus **533 e2e tests including every `accessibility` spec in that range passed** before that sweep was killed.

**THE SIGKILL WAS NOT UNRELATED AND WAS NOT THE OS,** and this is worth the paragraph because the failure signature is a trap. Eleven tests went red — `maintenance.spec.ts` ×4, `leases.spec.ts` ×3, `notice-to-vacate.spec.ts` ×2 and retries — and the sweep was killed deliberately, on the rule that a doomed run gets stopped rather than finished. **The cause was R-112 editing those exact files while the sweep was reading them**: two sessions were live in this repo at once, and `notice-to-vacate.spec.ts` was rewritten at 23:35:28 between two reads of it a minute apart — the first read said R-111, the second said R-112. Nothing in R-111's diff was involved; every failing file was one of R-112's nine. **`Killed: 9` names no culprit and neither does a wall of 1.0m timeouts** — the check that settled it was `ls /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/JetsamEvent-*.ips` (nothing for that minute) followed by `git status`, which is what exposed the concurrent session. One session per project is a rule for this reason: the second one's symptom is indistinguishable from a memory kill and from a real regression in whatever you just changed.

**What it left behind.**
- **No dark mode, deliberately.** If it is ever wanted it starts at `globals.css` with a palette and a toggle.
- **The rest of the audit's 75 findings.** R-112 below takes the tenant-portal blockers; angle ㉓, four more repeated-name sites and the portal's 16px floor are unowned.
